IN ARCADY. In yon hollow Damon lies, Lost in slumber deep. (Hush, hush, ye shepherd girls, Break not his sleep.) Phyllis passes tiptoe by; Whither is she hieing? (Peep, peep, ye shepherd girls, He for her is dying.) Now she pauses, now she bends, Ah, she kissed him purely. (Look away, ye shepherd girls, Frown, frown demurely.) See, he clips her in his arms, She who was the proudest. (Laugh, laugh, ye shepherd girls, Laugh, laugh, your loudest.) .—conise Monkhouse, in "Me Magazine of Art."

THE DEATH OF THE OLD YEAR. ' Full knee-deep lies the winter snow, And the winter winds are wearily sighing; -- Toll ye the church bell sad and slow, And tread softly and speak low, For the Ord Year lies a-dying. Old Year, you must not die; You came to us so readily, You lived with us so steadily, dld Year, you shall not die. Re lieth still: he doth not move: He will not see the dawn of day. He hath no other life above. He gave me a friend, and a true, true lovis, And the New Year will take 'em away. Old Year, you must not go; go long as you have been with us, Such joy as you have seen with us, Old Year, you shall not go. He froth'd his bumpers to the brim; A jollier year we shall not see. But tho' his eyes are waxing dim, And tho' his foes speak ifi of him, Be was a friend to me. Old Year, you shall not die; We did so laugh and cry with YOU, 'l've half a mind to die with you, Old Year, if you must die. He was full of joke and jest, But all his merry quips are o'er. To see him die, across the waste His son and heir doth ride post-haste, But he'll be dead before. Every one for his own. 'The night is starry and cold, my friend, aind the New Year blithe and bold, au friend, Comes up to take his own. How hard he breathes! over the snow I heard just now the crowing cock. The shadows flicker to and fro : The cricket chirps: the light burns low: 'Tis nearly twelve o'clock. Shake hands, 'before you die. Old Year, well dearly rue for you; What is it weean do for you? Speak out before you die. His face is growing sharp and thin, ALack I our friend is gone. *Close up his eyes: tie up his chin: Step from the corpse, and let him in That standeth there alone, And waiteth at the door. There's a new foot on the floor, my friend, And a new face at the door, my friend, A new face at the door. , Tannewseir.

Let us begin our heaven on-earth; and, being our >selves tempted, let us be pitiful and considerate and', generous in judging others.—.Tolm Page Hopps. ; Talkingof the importance of individuals to themselves, Douglas mentions a letter from a.servant-maid in which. ishe says •.--" I hear that it is all over London that I am about to leave my place." A man left a bony steed in the street, and coming back 1 ss short time afterwards discovered-thet a funny. youth; bad placed a card rgainst the fleshless ribs, bearing the bascription: " Oats-wanted—inquire within." "Sam, you are not honest. Why dia you put all the good peaches on the top of the measure, and the little dime's below?" "Same reason, ash, datfmakes de front of your house marble and the back gate chiefly slop bar'l, sal." An exasperating edtor being threatened with a coat of tar and feathers, said in his next issue----" The people in this town may break into somebody's ;henroost and steal the feathers, but we know that they am too stingy to buy the tar." "Do you know why you and George remind me of two shades of one colour?" aaked a young lady,ef a cam- panion who had been engaged for a good marry years. " No," was the reply. "111 tell you then. A• It's be- cause you don't match." A political orator, speaking of a certain general whom he professed to admire, said that on the field of battle he was always found where the bullets were thickest. "Where was that?" asked one of the auditors. "In the ammunition waggon, said anothM. Business is in a bad way! A stockbroker who had gone to meet Rothschild was relating his adventures Ito his friend, "Affairs must be in a very bad state, in- deed," said he. "I have been at Rothschild's. Even. they are suffering. On passing a half-open door I saw Madame Rothschild and her datighter. They were play- ing on the same piano!" A nervous man whose life was made miserable by the clattering of two blacksmiths, prevailed on each of them to remove by the offer of a liberal compensation. When the money was paid down he kindly inquired what neighbourhood they intended to remove to. "Why, sir," replied Jack, with a grin, "Tom Smith moves to my shop, and I move to his,, The guests at the boarding-house of the Widow Flap- jack, on Austin-avenue, still continue to grumble at their fare. Yesterday morning Gilhooley said at break- fast table to Mrs. Flapjack—" I notice that you have a vicious-looking dog in the yard. Does he bite?" "In- deed he does.' "Will you be kind enough to give him this tender loin beefsteak with my compliments. I'd like very much to see him bite it if you have no objec- t ons." . . . .

There is one point in every life at which all things ap- pear in their true colours. It is the point of death. All illusions vanish there. There are no false estimates of deeds in the light of that hour. The things we shall wish then that we had done are things we ought to have done. The things that will look fair and lovely as we sit in the gloaming of life's day are the things that are truly lovely. The things that will shame us then are the things that God condemns and which we ought not to have done.

A HEN'S MEMORY:A person living near Galt, Ontario, set some duck eggs under a hen. When they were li-itched the hen went about as merry as you please with the little ducks. One day, however, they came to a pool of water, and the ducks naturally went in for a swim. The hen got so frightened, and called in vain for them to come out. Next year duck eggs were put under the smile hen again, and as soon as they were hatched and she saw that her family were ducks she killed everyone of them._

Thu LAUGHING PLorr.—This is :not a flower that laughs, but one that creates laughter, if the printed stories of travellers are to be believed. It grows in Arabia, and is called the laughing plant, because its seeds produce effects like those produced by laughing gas. The flowers are of a bright yellow, and the seed- pods are soft and wooly, while thefieeds resemble small black beans, and only two or three grow in a pod. The natives dry and pulverise them, and the powder if taken in small doses makes the soberest.person behave like a circus clown or a madman, for he wilgdanc,e, sing, and laugh most boisterously, and cut the most fantastic capers and be in an uproariouslyi ridiculous' condition for about .an hour. When the :excitement ceases, the exhausted exhibitor of these antics falls asleep, and when he awakes he has not the slightest remembrance of his frisky doings. As smoking is supposed to be an innocent indulgence, and as it is customary with some people to relate the news of the day with cigars in theirimouths, and as the generality of smokers make anfawkward appearance) in c imsequence.of their ignorance of the theory of punctua- tien in smoking, the following 'system is recommended: —A simple puff serves for a comma (,) ; puff, puff, a (;) ; puff, puff, puff, a colon (:) ; six puffs, a period (.). .A pause, with a cigar left in :the mouth, r -presents a dash (—),longer or shorter in continuance. With the under lip raise the cigar almost against the nose for an exclammation ; and to express great emotion, even to the shedding of tears,' only raise, as before, the cigar to the end of the nose. For an interro- gation (?), it is only necessary to open the lips and draw the cigar round the corner of the mouth. Taking the agar. from the mouth and shaking the ashes from the pad is the conclusion of a paragraph; and throwing it into the fire is a final and stylish pause. Never begin a story with a half-finished cigar; for to light another while conversing is not only a breach of :politeness, but it interferes with the above system of punctuation, and d'stroys all energy of harmony and expression. THE ONLY Two 'Goan THINGS IN THE WORLD.-2ThO last fish which I shall mention is the oulachan, or candle fish (Osmerus pacifus), a species of smelt, which ascends the northern rivers in March. It is captured in great numbers by the 'lndians for food, but mere particularly for the purpose iof extracting the oil from its tissues. This oil, which is, when cold, of the consistency of palm- oil, is used forcooking, and is also eaten by the nattess. It has also 'the good qualities of cod liver oil without its nausea. Probably its use is the salvation of the natives ,cf that part of the toast where 'chest diseases are very common. So highly valued is dt by the Indians, that when they come to Victoria 'they always bring some boxes of it with them. One of' them remarked tome that there were'onlytwo good things in the world—" rum and oulachan oil "."'—" The Cousaties of the World.'" . Two Sines TO THE Quiiensett—" Tweet ! "tweet ! tweet!" What a noise they were making in theAvy-claci, tower, and under the eaves of the old church! What could it all mean? Were the swallows rejoicirg in the bright spring weather and in their return twtheir old • haunts, ET were they telling their acquaintances, the sparrows,the story of their wanderings, and exchang- ing ideas 'on the events that lad owner& in their absencet Evidently some knotty point wasauider dis- cussion, and a jackdaw lazily lapped his idid,_ gs and descended from the top of the •ateepU to learn what it was allahout. ." Hypocrite !" "Interloper r, • " Setting himself up for better than his neighbours.," 'were a few of the epithets which greeted ins ears as he alighted. "I hate Tour new-fangled ways I" chirped a matronly sparrow, whose ancestors had had their•nees in the ivy for generations. "Give me a 'window 'you can see throughl" " New-fangled ! my dear madam," replied the swallow in a patronising tone, "allow me to assure 'you that all the records -of antiquity would 'use in favour of our friend—" "Friend, indeed," and a perfect babble of sound issued from the old walls, as birds and insects combined in raising their voices against the new corner; for had they not each and all suffered in some way or another by his advent? "I confess I do not pretend) to understand him," said a large spider; "he is so-totally different from other windows of my acquaintance- Once on their sill I knew exactly at what angle to cast my thread, but with his wavy lead line, ugh !" and rotling4himself up into a ball he disappeared. "Understand him !I should think not indeed," chimed in a snail. "I flatter myself my ac- quaintance with him is closer than any,of. yours ; and— would you believe it? at first, afterlahotious considera- tion, I came to the conclusion he was blue, then yellow, and now positively I believe him to bared! Such incon- sistency is sickening." "Though needful may be for the beauty vf the whole," said the jackdaw, who had hitherto kept silence; but his remark called forth such a chorus of abuse that he slowly rose to- tlui summit of the tower, croaking forth about ' narrow-mincted preju- dice," and "two sides to every quarrel" The evening shadows closed in, the moon rose in the heavens, and as she threw her pale, cold light on the,painted window a murmur of complaint broke the midnight stillness. "0, why came if here ? Why am I so maligised, misjudged ? Why can I net proclaim to all the truths -so cleeply graven mi myself? Why cannot all see thetlaster's design shone forth by me ?" The moonbeams plaved around the sorrowful one and answered, "Are you not where the Architect would have you be? Did not He Arnow the limit of your influence? Let but the sun's -rays shine through you, and the story He has entrusted to your keeping will, in the colours He has designed,' fall forward on the prepared ground." . . . . "What a- lovely window!" exclaimed the elder of the two ladies whoen- tered the church a few days afterwards. "Howbeauti, fully the colours blend! You may think me fanciful,", she continued, "but do you, know, a window like that seems to me an apt symbol of our life, all .made of different pieces and Ohades joined together bpwhat we I call circumstances, aid to outsiders, and evesoomethises , to ourselves, with very little beauty to see' ia it„ er de- sign; but once let us within the vale, and illumined by t.-.. he light of God's loving purpose, we shall see-thatwe have all the time been working out His Likeness,xeflect- ' ling little by little His Image, and shall then be satisfied." --New Parables from Nature, by Lady Laura Hampton, in ' lite Quiver. TO WHOM WAS ST..IOIISAItSECOND EPISTLE ADDHESSED ? •••••-.1, ;Ake the letter, then, in its natural sense, as having been addressed to a Christian lady and her children. Some of those children the g_postle seems to have met 1 in OW of his visits of supewrision to the Churches of Asia. ;They may have been on a visit to some of their cousins in a neighbouring ei‘;'' and St." John—always attracted by sympathy towards the young—finding that they wane living as faithful Clatit,tian lives, writes news of thena•to their mother, whom he held in high esteem; and in writing seizes the opportunity to add some words of Christian teaching. That St. ithn should write to a . Chn4tan4stly has in it nothing esitraoreinary. Women like Prtscilk, Lydia and Phcebe played no small part in the early tweed oiiChristian truth. They represented that ennoblement of Christian Womanhood which was one of the owat results of Christian aareaching ; and they inspired ilbe Apostles with a warm sentiment of affection and esteem. That the lady &mild be left un- named is in accordance with the feelings of the day. It was against he common feelings both of Jews and Greeks that iirtuous matrons shotald be thrust into needless prominence. St. Paul indeed names them when occasion demands. In wring- to the Philippians, among -whom women occupied a more recognised position than among other Roman eommuni- ties, he Makes a personal appeal to the two ladies Euodias and Syntyche -; and he sends salutations to and from women among others. Yet he never wrote tletter, so far as we know, even teLydia or to Priscilla, to whom be was so much indebted -; and if ho had written each a letter—intended (as this letter of St. John's may well have been) for perusal by all the members of the church, and even meant to be read aloud to them in their con- gregation—it is probable that he would have left the name unmentioned. Much more would this have been thenatural feeling of St. John, who had lived most of his life in Jerusalem. He would have been less inclined to infringe on the seclusion which was the ordinary posi- tion of Eastern womanhood, because his experiences had been less cosmopolitan than that of his brother Apostles. Who the Elect Lady was we do not know, and never shall know. To suggest, as some have done, that she I may have been Martha, the sister of Lazarus, or the Mother of our Lord, is to be guilty of the idle and repre- hensible practice of suggesting theories which rest on the air, and are not oven worth the trouble of a serious refutation.—" The Early Days of Christianity." Corms.—All due precautions ought to be taken against catching cold, but it is folly to teach our children to look upon snow as on something frawlit with danger. It is dangerous, perhaps, to sit and shiver in it, or to walk and shiver in it, but to romp in it is life. On the other hand, danger lurks in the rain-clouds, in the damp air of a winter evening, and in the choking fogs and mists that creep up from and bang overkrivers. The only time when snow is really to be feared is when it is melting. A word or two about the theory and treat- ment of a common cold may not be out of place here. The blood, then, of the body is, in health, equally dis- tributed to all the organs--lungs, liver, skin, brain, &c. Now whatsoever disturbs the 12alance of the circulation causes illness. It is evident that cold, or a chill caught from sitting in a draught, will have this effect. For the blood is impelled inwards from the surface of the body towards important organe, which become over distended with blood (what we medical men term congestion)— If it be the lungs that are congested, very serious mis- chief will be the result; but it is more often the lining membranes of the throat and lungs, and these try to re- lieve themselves by discharging the watery portion of the blood. It is this that tickles, and causes the cough; it is merely water at first, but it becomes mattery at last--purulent, and as the discharge is increased, relief is found. Many, if not most, of the expectorants or cough mixtures we use have for their aim and object the increase of the discharge, in a natural manner, from the membrane lining the lungs, and the consequent de- crease of the congestion. Well, that is one plan we adopt for the cure of a cold, and the other is to endea- vour to restore the circulation by warmth of skin. The 1 hot or Turkish bath is invaluable at the onset of a cold, but as everyone cannot take it with safety, I can only recommend warmth in bed, rest; a light diet, and hot mustard and water to feet and legs at bedtime. But a child should not be treated to the foot bath unless over five years of age. Some opening medicine tends greatly to the cure. The best cough mixture should contain tincture of squills, a little paregoric, a little nitrate of potash, and some sweet nitre. Spirits of sweet nitre is a capital remedy in colds; dose, from ten drops to a tea- spoonful three times a day. This is the simplest treat- ment for the effects of told on the lungs, and that most in accordance with common sense. But it must not be forgotten that in colds caught from a chill, other organs as well as the lungs suffer; hence headaches, drowsi- ness, and a general feeling of being out of sorts. For 41 these the treatment we cannot do wrong in adopting consists of aperient medicine, the warm bath, rest, and low diet; but exercise must be taken, even in the house, else the circulation cannot be kept up. Walking briskly up and down the floor is a far wiser proceeding after a warm bath, taken during the day, than lying down on a sofa, probably to shiver. Remember this, too, that no one will catch cold out of doors who moves about _ , briskly, even among melting snow. And why? The • answer is obvious—it keeps up and retains the equili- brium of the circulation. If these remarks of mine on the effects of cold are too hard to be understood by young girls, I feel sure they will be appreciated by their mothers.—Girls' Own Paper. KAY'S COMPOUND OF LINSEED. Earl Cawdor was .elected president, 'aied Lord Kensingthn, Mr. W. Davies, M.P.,' tir Marteine Lloyd, Sir Owen Scourfield, and Mr. E. G. l'hillipps, of Picton Castle, vice-presidents. A set of rules., were adopted. _ - SILAGE IN &Tears.—The plan cif compressing green (Odder in stacks above ground, instead of in silos, long practised to some extent by Dutch farmers, has been tried in England during the pate season. In our last; iSSIMI we gave a report by a Hampshire farmer of a suce' ceseful experiment of the kind. another experiment of the same description has been tarried out with the help of an elaborate system of mechanical pressure, which appears quite en unnecessary ;expense. The explanation of the preservation of the fodder is that it became so solid that the air could not penetrate more than about nine inches at the sides of the stack, and not much mere at the top. It will be advisable for all who try the plan to fiithe stack at a distasies from any, other stack or any building, as a little hitch in the arrangement might easily led' to the heating, and ultimate firing, of the fodder: THE AGRICDITTTRAL CR/SlB IN THE UNITED STATPS.— Almost every week for same time past there has been some very striking evidence of the disastrous character of the agricultural crisis in the United States, calmed by the great fall in the price of wheat, and some ef that evidence has been copied into this journal. In the face of this evidence, it would be folly to deny that American farmers are selling wheat•et a loss. The cost of produc- tion varies in different -States, according to local esti- mates, from. 40 cents tezelollar, and none of those esti- mates include all the items that should be. 'charged against the wheat crop. .But, apart from the probability of nearly all the estimates being too low, there is the fact that the price of wheat is everywhere belew the estimate of its cost. There are many people in this country who believe that wheat can be grown for next to nothing in the United States, as if the farmers got their labour as well as their land for nothing, and stole their capital. Probably nothing but a decrease in the acreage of wheat in America. will convince such people that they have been mistaken, and they will not, have to wait long for the 'official statement of such decrease. One of the best authorities on the subject, Mr. Sidway, of Chicago, who is now in this country, fully confirms the statements as to the unremunerative ch.aracter of the wheat growing butiness, the desertion of farms in parts of Dakota and some other States, and the decrease in the area planted with winter wheat, as compared with that of last year. He estimated the decrease at'2s per cent. The January report of the United States Depart- ment of Agricultureew ill give an authoritative estimate. The Eldemlie is the first steamer that has been specially built for this trade, and the voyage Sei,st completed is the first she has made. She is a fine vessel of about 3,800 tons, coristructed by the Palmer shiP- building- and Iron Company, of Jarrow-on-Tyne, !or Messrs. Martin, Turnbull, and Co., of Glasgow. Her owners were induced by Mr. John:Reid, of Elderslie, Oamarie South New Zealand, to give the order for her building, that gentleman having undertaken to load her 'with mutton for England for several years. Frozen mutton has never before been received in this country., directly at least, from the district of Oamaru. It may be mentiened that in 1881 no such meat arrived here from New Zealand, and only 13,771 carcases from .Anstralia. In 1882 we got 8,840 carcases from New Zea- land, and 45,087 from Australia. Steel, representing the builders of the v,essel,-; and Mr. Laugetcle.—The Chairman made a feeir xemmers, in the course cif which referring to the time required es build the new ships which the Government have determined to add to the Royal,Nassy, he said that the Elderslie was constructed in five months. (Hear, hear.)—The -three present sources of snpply of muttcn—New Zealand, Australia, and the River Plate—are by no means eti a par as to the mutton they send us. The last-named is; declared the most inferior of the three, while the Aus- tralian carcasses are smaller, more muscular, and lees juicy than the sheep New Zealen.d farmers send us. It has lately been pointed out, however. that the New Zealanders, if not subject to the severe droughts of Australia, and enjoying much more ' luxuriant pastures. are burdened by very heavy taxation, and that their flocks suffer in many districts from cold and exposure, and the attacks of a bird of the parrot tribe, which eats into the back of the sheep, so that there is sonic limit to the competition to be looked for in that direction. FARMERS AND SPARROWS.—MT. Theodore Wood, of 5, Selwyn-terrace, Upper Norwood, writes to the Daily News :—" I was very sorry to see in a recent impression I of the Daily News that Miss E. A. Ormerod is taking up , the old crusade against the common sparrow, and has , even subscribed to a fund for its extirpation, Miss Ormerod's exalted position as entomologist to the Royal Agriculturist Society' doubtless entitles her opinion to a certain amount of respect, and it is therefore the more to be regretted that she should have committed herself to an exploded theory. It is true enough that the spar- row is Mischievous to a certain extent during the autumn and winter months, but its services as an insect destroyer in the earlier part of the year fully compen- sate for the damage which it causes later on. A pair of these birds have been known to carry to their nest an average of forty grubs per hour throughout the day, and more than three thousand in the course of the week. ;And surely we have had instances enough of the results ;following upon even the partial extermination of the ,bird. Have we not yet learnt that Nature knows how to preserve her own balance? Kill the insect destroyers and the insects must increase, as has been proved only ; too often in this and other countries. At Maine, for in- stance, the total destruction of the sparrows was ordered by Government, the consequence being that in the fol- lowing year even the trees were stripped of their leaves. We have recognised the fact in the case of, the rook (which even Miss Ormerod admits is an ally of the farmer) that a bird which is injurious at one season may be so beneficial at another as to far more than compen- sate for the mischief which it has caused; and why not also with the sparrow ?" ME PROPOSED ESTABLISII3IENT OF INDI7STRIAL Vzt- uas.—lf the neW movement for promoting the estab- lishment of industrial villages comes to anything, it may be developed in a manner advantageous to agriculture. The idea is to relieve the overcrowding in the large towns and cities by establishing villages in which manir-1 factures and home handicrafts may be carried on, in connection with cottage or co-operative farms. It is lobvious that this plan might be developed either to the ' advantage er disadvantage of farmers. If it should be so managed as to diminish the existing supply of labour in the agricultural districts, it should draw townspeople into the 'country to a much greater extent than it would attract 'rural labourers, the result could scarcely fail to be satisfactory in all respects, supposing it to be in itself-succ,essful. In the first placethe increase of popu- lation in rural centres would create improved local markets for farm produce; and, secondly, it would pro- bably afford additional labour at busy agricultural sea- sons. If most of the wOrkmea had plots of land, it would be as desirable for 'them as for the large farmers to have their manufacturing work carried on chiefly if not exclusively in the late auitumn or winter and early spring. Then we should have what is so sadly needed —a new means of employment for farm hands at the seasons when only a portion of the men on a farm can be profitably employed. In districts where arable land is likely to be nearly all laid down in permanent pasture there is of course an opening for industry that would give employment to labourers all the year round. PLASTER OF PARIS •AS A TOP-DRESSING.—One great use of sulphate of lime de-hydrated or of the common plaster, is for the purpose of top-dressing upon the lucerne, trefoil, sanfoin, and other artificial grasses. This method of using it prevails to a very great extent, throughout France and the United States, but it is com- paratively unknown in this country. In the north-west of France the farmers use the plasZer in equal quantities with the seed sown, or 4cwt. to the acre. It is sprinkled gently over the grass crops, and the best time for em- ploying it is immediately beforea shower of rain. This dressing requires to be renewed every year, but the re- sults in produce are startling, se great is the difference in the weight of the grass crcps. Some experiments have been made with the English gypsum, but these have not been satisfactory; and to insure success, the French gypsum raised in the north-west of France should be employed; it is from this gypsum that our own well-known brand of plaster of Paris is manufac- tured. Many people are of the opinion that drones are simply createdt,o,be killed, and are of no :use except to eat the honey—a notion that I would like Ito, see dispelled. Of all insects I know none is more use- dill than the bee. Many serve a doubleoand, in fact, many purposes, some of which *exam see,the beginning and the end, but with the bee it Is different,-co manifold ore the purposes it serves. We eee it enter a,flower for the ostensible purpose of robbing it of its nectar, but whilett is so doing it is perhaps fanconscionab:e that it is at-the same time fertilising and gross-fertilising fruit blossoms and flowers, which will in a time give plea- sure and profit to many. I leave it to an abler pen than mine to fully describe the many uses .ce the bee and Its produce; but I must try to impress the enemies of tha drone with its usefulness. Erery- body who ,keeps bees knows that but few drones accompanyeither first or second swarms, while the old stock has many. It has been thought by some that the lazy drone, a,s he is termed, is too great a glutton to leave a well-filled larder and migrate with the swarm to an empty house. I look upon this in quite a different light. My ppinion is that, as is often the ease when a swarm issues., theme are not enough bees left to hatch the brood, which but for the presence of the drones would die. These drones, though taking no part in the in- ternal economy of the hive, increase thc heat and moisture so essential to the brood in an immature state. Both books and people teach that drones are killed at a certain period, but this, though partially true, is misleading. If the weather becomes wet and cold after the young queens have been served, and sometimes before it, drones are often killed or put out af the hive; but if the weather continues fine and the bees are collecting much honey, such as they do in a season like this has been at the heather, the drones are allowed to live. Their presence got only assists to hatch the brood through the neat generated, but materially assists in comb-formation, now more required than ever, as the honey is more plentiful land the demand for comb-hoaey greater than formerly. Thus we see not only a double but a treble purpose and use in the drone, which is liable to be lost sight of by many,—Lanarkshire Beekeeper in Journal of Horticulture.

div.head: DEATH ROLL OF 1884.
div.p: THE DEATH ROLL OF 1884.

The deaths of the year have not included any reigning Sovereign except the Duke of Brunswick, unless King Cetewayo be classed as one; but the Royal houses of Europe have nearly all been thrown into mourning by the death of the young Duke of Albany, the Prince of Orange, the Empress Dowager (Maria-Anna) of Austria, Prince George of Saxony, the Landgrave of Hesse, and one of the Saxe-Coburg Princes. The English aristoc- racy has sustained some very severe losses during the year, including the Duke of Buceleuch, the Duke of Wel- lington' the Duchess of Somerset, the Marquises of Hert- ford, Londonderry, and Cholmondeley, the Dowager Countess of Shrewsbury and Talbot, the Earls of Sdnd- wich, Cowley, Lauderdale, and Scarborough, Earl Gros- venor, Viscount Torrington, Lord Ampthill, Lady Bind- port, Lord Stafford, arid the Honourable Gilbert Leigh. The names of Lords Ampthill and Cowley might have been included among the public men who have died during the year—such as Sir Bartle Frere, Mr. Fawcett, Mr. Milner Gibson' Mr. T. W. Henley, at home; and Mid- hat Pasha, M. Rouher' Signor Sella, Herr Lasker, Count von Usedom, and Mr. Wendell Phillips abroad. The Church of England has lost many distinguished members, including the Bishop of Ripon the Deans of Gloucester and Bangor, the Provost and Vice-Provost of Eton (Dr. Goodford and the Rev. G. J. Dupuis), Canons Girdlestone and Hume, and the Bishop of Kilmore in Ireland; while the Dissenting sects have lost, among other men of note, Dr. Angus Smith, the Rev. Baldwin Brown, and Mr. W. H. Charming. The Armenian Patri- arch (Monsignor Nerses) has also died during the year; as have, in the Roman Catholic Church, the Cardinal Archbishop of Toledo and Cardinal Bilio, who was in at- tendance upon the Pope. The Rev. Mark Pattison might have been included amongst the deceased ecclesiastics; but he belongs rather to the battalion of men of letters, which has lost during the year Mr. A. Hayward, Mr. Blanchard Jerrold, Mr. T. Chenery, Mr. Charles Read, Mr. J. D. Lewis, Mr. Calverley (the University Tutor), Mr. Home (the poet), Mr. H. J. Byron, and Mr. Bromley-Davenport, M.P., at home; while abroad the deaths of Count d'Haussonville, M. J. B. Dumas, and M. Mignet has created vacancies in the French Academy; and the names of MM. Quicherat and Paul Lacroix, and of H. Laube, the novelist, will be familiar to many English readers. M. B. J. Dumas be- longed as much to the scientific as he did to the literary world, and science has sustained no greater loss during the year; though Dr. Voelcker and M. Wurtz were both eminent chemists; while Dr. Schlegel, Nilo committed suicide, was an eminent Dutch naturalist. The deaths of Mr. Justice Williams and of Mr. Long. field, ex-Judge in Ireland, were the most noteworthy in the legal world; and medicine has not to deplore the death of more than one famous man, Sir Erasmus Wil- son. The mortality among military and naval men has, upon the other hand, been very heavy, for Generals Sir W. Codrington, A. Cunynghame, and Sir D. Russell, Ad- mirals Sir S. S. Pasley, Sir Rodney Mundy, and 11. C. Glyn in the English services, and Generals Fleury, Schramm (France), Wimpffen (Austria), and Todleben (Russia), and Admiraj Fourichon (France), have all died since the beginning of the year. The deaths of painters, sculptors, &c., include those of Bastien-Lepage, Be Nittis, llans Mackart, Richter, and F. Hon, R.A., while in the musical and dramatic world such names as Sir Michael Costa, Victor Masse, Marie Litton, Fanny Elssler, and the Frezzolini, deserve special mention. The sporting world has lost Mr. Caledon Alexander, Sim Ternpleman the jockey, Lord Mostyn, and Sir Richard Bulkeley ; and Paul Morphy, the chess player; Delmonico, the New York restaurant- keeper; Count Pahlen, the friend and companion of Talleyrand ; Bass the brewer, and Mr. Robert Grimston, the great cricketer, have also died in the course of the year.

ARY 10. 1885 COTTAGE GARDENING

The past few days have been unusually favourable for conducting all kinds of work that required frequent movements over the ground. Besides being best for the ground the operator is able to go upon it with ease and comfort. The pruning of black currants having been completed we had some light manure wheeled amongst them, but left in heaps for the time being; as spreading it before all the frost is out would be shutting in the cold for a longer period than nature herself would do it. Apart from that, we thought it best to make sure of the wheeling, consequently we did not wish to , delay an hour by staying to spread. Some portions I were frozen when wheeled, and became more so in a few hours after being conveyed on the ground, which would have interfered with the regular disposal of the material. It should be understood that we do not put it on the ground with the view of digging or forking it in, for we do not approve of the practice except where the space between the rows admits of some intermediate crop, when the ground underneath the branches should be left intact. If the space between the rows only admits of a person passing between, it is evident that there is no space for a crop. On wet heavy soils the space be- tween the rows should be a few inches lower than that which the trees cover, and a channel may also be dug six inches deep. If the soil is thrown under the trees it will assist to raise that part, and after it has been broken small and levelled the manure may be spread on the top. The object of the channel is to prevent an ac- cumulation of surface water and so starve the surface roots, which are really the most valuable. Gardeners lay great stress on the importance of encouraging sur- face roots in all fruit trees. During the operation of picking the fruit, the actions of birds and the influence of the elements, the channel becomes nearly full by the end of the year, and will of course require re-opening. Tan FRONT GARDEN.—Last week we enumerated some of the materials in general use for live edgings for walks, and expressed our preference for thrift. Now as there are several species of thrift, it will be as well to state that the one selected for this purpose is the common one (Arineria Vulgaris), of which there are again four varie- ties. The best are the rose and the red, but all are use- - ful and pretty when planted on rockwork, or used to cover dry banks, where few plants would succeed. One of tho characteristics of all the species is that they do not succumb to drought so readily as the majority of plants. When it is intended to plant thrift, the ground should be made moderately firm by treading a space the width of the two feet and finish it off with the spade by making it slope to the walk and slightly higher than it. The row should be planted about two inches from the walk, and the plants in small patches abeut the same distance apart. When well raised above the walk the plants continue to grow for years. Probably the best of all edgings is a combination of living and dead materials, which could be carried out in the following manner : Assuming the ground to be prepared as for planting thrift, arrange on its surface some rugged stones, or clinkers of various sizes, so as to allow a-sufficient num- ber of interstices to receive soil in which to plant thrift in each space. In this case planting ina straight line should be avoided, and an easy, natural style selected, and the plants fixed at such distances as not to form a line when fully grown. They may, therefore, vary in distance from eight inches to one foot. In time they will root and embrace the stones and soil, and maintain them in one solid mass. Many of the saxifrage and hardy sedums are suitable plants for this purpose, and would have a pleasing effect. TEM Wirreow.—How much water shell I give .such and melt plant? is one of the most perplexing questions we have addressed to us by others as well as those inter- ested in window gardening. Now, were we asked.how the inquirer could tell when a plant required water, we should not feel so embarrassed, and our ;task of giving a satisfactory reply would not be quite so hopeless. When a plant is dry, the pot on the outside -will appear and feel , dry, and if such a pot is tapped with the -knueldesowith the hand partially open, at will have a hollow ring. This is a sure indication that the soil is really dry. The particles of soil on the surface will also feel-dry,when watering is required. Deving satis- fied ourselves that the plant requires water, ,the,quan- tity is easily determined. The surface of the soil in pots is from onedialf to two inches below the rim, the latter usually allowed for plants in 12in. pots, those in the window seldona,exceeding of an inch. If this spacels filled with water it is, as a rule, found suffieient to satu- rate the soil, and4he best evidence that it Las alone so is to see itcome cut at the bottom of the pot,

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRYTHE BREEDING OF TABLE FOWLS.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY- THE BREEDING OF TABLE FOWLS.

Those who wake the most profit out of the breeding of table fowls endeavour to get their chickens on to the market before the Ist of June. The Derby Day, gene- rally the last week in efe.,,y, marks the highest tide of prices in London. Alter it is past they very rapidly go down, until within a meanie or six weeks chicken n be bought for as naany pence almost as they would have commanded shillings previous to the great saturnalia. This state of affairs influences the prices more or less all over the kingdom, for whilst .they are so high, of course, London draws the beet from everywhere within reach. Thus if the poultry breeder desire to make his present pursuit profitable, he should have his birds hatched suf- ficiently early to permit their maturity in May. To do this, as they will not be fit for killing until they are 12 or 14 weeks old, he must have them batched by the first week in February at latest. So that no time should be last by those who intend tb have a supply of spring thickens to put on the market at the time named. peeklings can be killed at seven or eight weeks old, so that there is not such an imperative need to have them hatched at once, except that the earlier they are the rarer they will be. In either case, pens should be made up forthwith, and as a week should be allowed before eggs are used for hatching from hens so mated, there is no time to lose. If pullets. only are available, then a vigorous two-year-old mate should be given to them, as it would be risky depending upon an older bird for fer- tilising eggs so early in the year. In fact, it would be safer to have an 1883 autumn hatched cock that has not run with hens before, than one two years old which has been already employed for breeding. We prefer two- year-old hens for breeding stock birds, but for chickens to be killed pullets are better, as they lay earlier and better than the others. These are matters, however which must be guided by the circumstances of every poultry yard, but it is well, as far as possible, to conform to the suggestions already given. A few words may here be of service as to the beet breeds for table purposes. That there are best breeds no one can doubt, and those who have a market to sup- ply will find it to their advantage to keep one of the breeds, either pure or crossed. What is wanted is a plump-breasted fowl, of moderate size, with light bones, and one that will mature rapidly. All these are neces- sary qualities, and when found combined, as they are in some breeds, form a perfect table fowl. But some of the breeds that can claim these properties are delicate un- certain soils, and this facts needs to be known, or a very grave mistake may be made. The breeds which we should class as those distinctively table fowls are Dorkings, French, Game (both English and Indian), and Malays; but to these may be added some others, such as Langshan e; Plymouth Rocks, and Scotch Grays, though they aro scarcely equal to the first named. But on farms a general useful fowl is often pre- ferred—one which is good for the table and at the same time a decent layer. Dorkings are undoubtedly the best of all our English breeds if bred pure, but it has the serious drawback of being delicate and unable to withstand the effects of cold, clay soil, or exposed situations. It can be kept on the higher lands of North and East Lancashire without diffi- culty, but in the lower and consequently-damper portions, it is hardly so suitable. Of the four varieties of Dorkings, the coloured and silver greys are the largest, but the cuckoos and the whites are the hardiest. The Game fowl comes next, but it is small and its flesh rather dark, on which accouut many persons object to it. Its flesh is very firm, but rather dry. It is very hardy, and can be kept almost anywhere. Crossed with the Dorking, say a brown red game cock put to coloured or silver grey Dorking hens, or, if size is not so imperative a consider- then, to White Dorking hens, the produce is about the best for table purposes that can be obtained. Where the place is suitable, this is a crossing we can thoroughly recommend. The use of the Indian Game or Malay is ' preferred by some breeders to the brown red Game, and from the specimens exhibited at both the Dairy and Bir- mingham Shows, in which one or other of these varieties had a share, tbere can be no doubt that they are very valuable in crossing for the production of table fowls. Of the French breeds, all or any may be used, either alone or for crossing. The best is La Fleche, but it un- fortunately has the same failing as the Dorking, namely, inability to withstand a cold, damp soil. Much may be done to harden the breed by giving the birds full free- dom, allowing them to roost in the trees if they wish to do so, but yet we should not recommend the breed on low, damp ground. Creves come next. They are much hardier, and can be kept almost anywhere. They make good table fowls, growing rapidly and having fine white flesh. Their legs are dark, as are those of La Fleche, which is a drawback for roasters, but not so much as it used to be. Both La Pleche and Crews may be im- proved by crossing with Game, or Langshan, or even Brahma, and this will have the effect of strengthening the progeny. Houdans are also a first-rate breed, but not equal to either of the other French varieties men- tioned. It is a much better layer, but does not Mature so quickly or fatten so well. Whilst eminently a farmer's fowl from its intrinsic merits, it cannot be pronounced most suitable for early chickens. There are several other French breeds, such as La Bresse, Courtes Pattes, Le Maus, &c., which are useful table fowls, bit these are not to be readily obtained in this country, and can- not be said to be within reach of the fanner. Of the other breeds named, namely, the Langshan, the Plymouth Rock, and the Scotch Greys, .the first and last are the best for rapidly maturing and colour of flesh. The flesh of the Langslia n is beautifully white, and in the right place also. The breast is long and deep, and whilst it has scarcely the fine flavour of one or two other breeds, it is decidedly superior to the average run of chickens. Of the Scotch Grey, almost the same may be said. The Plymouth Rock grows to a good size, but is slower about it, and the flesh is rather yellow, though I very good in flavour and quality. Of course, in some I

places size is the first consideration, and when quantity, I not quality, is demanded then the best thing is to meet it by crossing the Dorking with the Brahma, or La Fleche or Creve with the Brahnaa. This will give the required size, with good meat, but much inferior to those crosses we have been recommending. Of the two varieties of Brahmas, the Lights are the best for crossing, but all of I the Cochin Or Brahma races give the yellow tinge to the ;flesh.

• SEASONABLE HINTS. It will be found of decided advantage at this season Of the year, especially 'where laying and breeding pens are kept, to have the side of the house on which the window is placed facing the south, so that the inside of the house may receive as much of the sun's ray's as possible. Many will be surprised at the difference be- tween the warmth of the house facing this way and if looking north, and the inmates will repay the.trouble and forethought -by greater productiveness. Such a po- sition is always the best, but specially so in the winter and spring. A sheet of thick glass let into the roof is also -S good thing, if where it will catch the sunshine,

THE MISADVENTURES OF AN AMATEUR CONJUROR. ' What could have induced me, Algernon Biles, a part- ner in a banking-house, middle-aged, sober-minded, and Yorkshireman—what could have induced me to go in for amateur conjuring is a mystery to myself, even now. It was a chance visit to Trotterham Fair, last October, that began the mischief, for having same spare time on my hands, I thought I might as well have a look at the shows, and took a turn -among the booths accordingly, including that of Professor Chimborazo, the Wizard of ' the Appenines. The professor was a flabby little man, in a seedy dress suit touch too large for him, and he might have been more particular about his finger nails; but his dexterity was something marvellous. The way coins disappeared and reappeared at the tips of his fin- gers, the wonders that he did with a greasy pack of cards, and the manner in which he rolled twolabbits into one, and produced bowl after bowl of fish from a dirty red pocket-handkerchief, seemed to me to savour of the supernatural. I had seen conjurors before, but not since my boyish days, and certainly none to compare with this man in dexterity. I watched him open- mouthed, and caught myself reflecting, as he repeatedly explained to us that the whole secret lay in the quick- ness of the 'and, which deceived the eye, What a jolly thing it would be if I could acquire the same dexterity, and astonish my friends with similar marvels !" The thing looked so remarkably easy! Chancing, as I passed out, to see the professor standing at the entrance, I in- vited him to accompany me to the hotel opposite. The upshot of the interview was that I agreed to pay a couple of guineas for a course of lessons in the art and mystery of legerdemain. After the lessons the profes- sor bade me not be discouraged. 4. Never you fear, dear boy, just you stick at it, with an 'our or two of practice every day. In particler, mind you practice palming. You ought never to be without a egg, or a 'arf-crown, or a 'andkerchief, concealed in the palm of your 'and. And when you feel you're getting your 'and in, run up to London, and go in for a nice little fit-up of apparatus at Affable's." I bade adieu to the professor, and did my best to carry out his instructions as to practice, particularly in reference to palming. I nearly always had a half-crown or other object concealed in the palm of my right hand. I found, however, that this had its inconveniences. For instance, I was unfortunate enough seriously to offend one of our county magnates, Sir Gregory Harbottle, by transferring half-a-crown to his hand (quite uninten- tionally), in shaking hands one evening after I had been dining with him. For some time nothing would per- suade him but that I intended to insult him by offering the half-crown in payment for my dinner, and though I did my best to explain, he has treated me with marked coolness ever since. On another occasion, in the parlour of our bank, I accidentally let fall a new laid egg just at the feet of one of our best customers. He drew out the greater part of his balance the next day, and I don't think he has ever regained complete oonfidence in our firm. However, by degrees I was acquiring a certain amount of familiarity with the movements taught me by the professor, and I took the first opportunity of a visit to London to make a fair start by purchasing a little apparatus, including a handsome table, a couple of side-tables and a couple of chairs, also very handsome, and each possessing special magical virtues; and a demon's head, fixed on a brazen pillar, warranted to do unheard-of things—to nod for "yes," move from side to -side for "no," tell fortunes, perform card tricks, smoke a pipe, blow a whistle—in fact, do everything but talk. My new poseaesions stirred me to fresh enthusiasm. ff practised assiduously all the movements which Chim- borazo had taught me, and found, to my great satisfac- tion, that I was really acquiring a certain amount of dexterity. I took my groomaem Stokes, into my confi- deuee, and did my bent to train him to act as my assist- ant; but I found him desperately thick-headed. After th.ree months of pretty eonstant practice, / took an op- portunity, at a small evening party, to volunteer a little legerdemain. I succeeded tolerably well, and repeated this performance on two or three different occasions, in each ea-se, however, only attempting small drawing- room tricks. I was gradually gaining confidence, and rashly determined one morning to make the plunge, and attempt a regular stage "show.-" The committee of our Mechanics' Institute, of which I was a vice-president, ,were desirous of giving a charity concert; but the local talent was getting rather stale, and they found great difficulty id making out an attractive programme. Here was my opportunity. I took heart of grace, and boldly offered to fill up the second part with a magical enter- tainment. When the eventful evening arrived the Town Hall was positively crammed. The sight of such an assemblage was very gratifying, but at the same time rather trying to a nervous man; and I now began to realise for the first time that I was nervous, painfully nervous. I had been practising diligently for the last fortnight, and had been doing my utmost to coach up Jem Stokes to the proper performance of his duties; but he a most unsatisfactory assistant. Ho had an unhappy knack of always pulling the wrong string, or, if he by a happy chance, got hold of the right one, he was pretty sure either to pull it at the wrong time, or to forget to pull it at all. However, I had so care- fully written down his duties, and hammered them so persistently into his head, that thought he could hardly make any mistake. That I myself should make any I deemed a much more remote contingency. But pride comes before a fall. As the curtain rose, I canter forward, wand in hand, and was received with a tremendous round of applause. I had prepared a neat little opening speech, which I had rehearsed some scores of times before the looking-glass, and which I felt would earn a well-merited round of ap- plause. And I have no doubt it would have done so, but I never delivered it; for when it came to the point, I really couldn't remember, for the life of me, what it was. What I did say was something like the following:— "Ladies and gentlemen—that is, respected friends and fellow-townsmen, or, I should rather say, Mr. Mayor, ladies, and gentlemen—l have come—l mean to say I am here—in point of fact. lam going, with your per- mission, if you will allow me, to show you this evening a few experiments, illustrating the superiority of mind over matter" (this was a fragment of my original speech), "which I propose—that is, I intend—with your permis- sion, to phoW you this evening. You are probably aware, ladies and gentlemen—that is, you know, or possibly you—you may not know—that the quickness of the hand, when very quick indeed, deceives the eye, because the eye—no, I mean the hand—travels faster than the hand—l should say the eye, can follow. If your hands are quicker than my eyes—that is—no; I mean if your eyes are quicker than my hands—why, of course, you'll See, exactly 'how it's done.' But if, on the contrary, your eyes—l mean my hands—are quicker than your eyes, why, then—why, then, of course, my hands being the quickest, you won't see anything at all. I will not detain you further, ladies and gentlemen, with introduc- tory observations, but will at once proceed to—to—in point of fact, to show you a few conjuring tricks." I felt myself getting hotter and hotter, but every one applauded, and I plunged desperately into my first trick. Its effect was, or rather ought to have been, as follows: ...rive cards being drawn, are placed in a pistol, and fired at an elegant five-pointed star, when the five chosen cards are seen to attach themselves one to each point of the star. This feat mainly depends on the performer being able to "force" the right cards in the first instance —not a very easy matter even for a professional con- juror. I succeeded with three, but failed as to the other two. When the pistol was fired four cards appeared, but two of them were wrong ones; and the fifth card, from setae cause or other, did not appear at all. This made me hotter still; but the audience nevertheless ap- plauded, and I went on. My second and third tricks passed without any serious hitch, and I proceeded, with increased confidence, to perform the well-known, but always popular, trick of the inexhaustible bottle. My bottle was of large size, and of the very best construc- tion. It was arranged to give port, sherry, rum, milk, a considerable variety of liqueurs, and, finally, a small quantity of castor oil, which I intended to administer to some small boy by way of finish; and in order to bring the demands to a termination I had produced sherry, rum, and milk with success, and was beginning to feel quite cock-a-hoop, when, as ill-luck would have it, Sir Gregory Harbottle, the president of the institute, and the victim of the "half-crown" incident, entered the room. In the hope of propitiating him, I invited him to take a glass of prime old port, which I knew was a special weakness of his. He assented, and I poured it out accordingly; but, as ill-luck would have it, or from some carelessness on my own part, a small portion of the castor oil flowed into the glass with it. He took a mouthful, made a grimace as if he was going to have an apoplectic fit, then spat it out on the floor. Bursting with rage, he said, "This is the second time, sir, you have made me the victim of your confounded practical jokes. If you try it a third time, by Heaven, I'll horse- whi p you!" I endeavoured to apologize, but it was use- less; he marched out of the hall, and I could hear him vowing vengeance half-way up the village. After this little incident I thought it better not to offer any more refreshment out of the enchanted bottle; arid this time everybody was too horrified to applaud. I said a few words expressive of my regret at the accident, and passed on to my next trick, whicliwas one I had learnt of Chimborazo, and consisted of mixing the ingredients for a "Welsh rabbit" in a tin saucepan, cooking them over a fire made in a borrowed hat, and then producing,

not the customary "Welsh rabbit," or "rarebit," but n real living rabbit. If the trick is properly performed' the hat runs no rislc of injury; but my nerves had heels.._ so shaken by the previous contretemps that I omitted r_ extinguish the flames at the right moment, and I savi,,,s my horror, that the hat (a new one, belonging. to local doctor) was frizzled internally in a most alarra!"6 n:kanner. -I tried to convey to the owner, in.returning it, that I would set matters nroiht with but I could not make him u erstand my. eignals, and„ I saw him, with a very lugubrious expression of comaen ~ Once, pointing out the &Wage tO hiS iMIDOCUate neigh . bours. This did not tend to restore my equitnimity. next trick was that of the well-known " fish.bow.l.% This I had practised in private till I felt that I nsu thoroughly mastered it ; and had I not been upset by InY previous misfortunes, I am quite sure I could ha," ' performed it with complete success; but I had by thiS time lost my nerve, and thought of nothing but setting the whole thing over. The result was that, in prodnet ' the first bowl, I shot the entire contents—water, , and all—over the legs of the vicar, who sat in the iron! row. The good old 'man, I honestly believe, felt 111017. for my shame and confusion than 'his own discomfol'. He entreated me not to mention it, assured me that au_ cidents would happen, and so on ; but his Christit._ forbearance could hardly be expected to extend to slf.. ting out the remainder of the performance in wet .tre'st sers, and he retired. Had he entertained the rac.)th vengeful feelings, he might have been fully satisfied `771. the ;Veniesis that immediately overtook me, for. in ;cc deavouring to produce the second bowl, I accidenta, pulled off the cover in my pocket. There was an inst?_ rush of water, and the audience were edified by If. spectacle of a miniature Niagara proceeding from region of my coat-tails. I could have sunk into earth; thiS indeed, if the platform had suddenly opened atilhe swallowed me up, I should have regarded it as greatest boon that could have been conferred uponTuit But no such refuge was open to me. Shakspere , us that a man "may smile, and smile, and be a villays.o I daresay he may. To my mind "to smile, and snits. as I had to do, while conscious of a meandering Wel running down my right leg and making little pools the floor wherever I paused, is a far more diffic achievement. I reflected with delight that I had now come W 0:4 7 last trick, the Enchanted Head, which was to cenclll.,t the performance, and this being chiefly mechanical, a faint hope that here, at any rate, there would be failure. To my horror, however; I found, on going 7,,f hind the scenes, that Jein Stokes, on whom this iteo.,,. the programme chiefly depended, and who was as ous as myself, had been keeping his courage up by ine'tri, of the liquors I had provided for the inexhaustible beta& and was, in plain language, decidedly tipsy. I ra,,40 him rub his head and face with a wet towel to sobeL,'" s as far as possible, and I placed him at his post, scileg strongly worded caution, and taking up the clenn,,,,e, head, went forward, and placed it on the table. artistic excellence of the head, which was really a mu.,`,—,ci in its way, produced an instant round of applause, c "'O, I began to hope that / should at any rate score one su,„ cess to finish up with. I said, "The head will nowss lute the company." Instead of making, as it sh°oo. have done, a succession of graceful inclinations, the,.e founded thing opened its mouth to its utmost ex":,r. and roiled its eyes from side to side in a grossly iorid tinent manner. The audience, however, rather enjoL, this act of rebellion, and applauded lustily. I said WI "Ladies and gentlemen, the head will now answer a 9 /no questions you like to put. to it, nodding for yest , mg from side to side for 'no,' and blowing this w. (which I stuck in its mouth accordingly) i" to ilaw"lft numbers." Questions were accordingly :asked, and Imo; head proceeded to answer, but quite on its own he'3lf;te. to speak, and without the smallest regard to iny,Y,Jr vious instructions to Stokes. It gave the age Of Horrocks, the dentist (rather a swell ;in his very 'sensitive on this point), at seven years more he himself owns to ; and repeatedly maintained Mrs. Toiler, the saddler's wife, had three children' known Toiler family consisting only. of two. Tow...t who is unfortunately of an extremely jealous temQsl",,,., ment, showed so much annoyance, not dimhaishea the universal laughter around, that Mrs. T. was matey carried out in hysterics. In fact, the heau.n hayed in such a disgraceful manner, that it wasquit relief to me when something or other suddenly ga '- way, and its manifestations ceased altogether. How the performance terminated I scarcely knoW.,d have a dim idea that I punched Jem Stokes's head hell 7; the scenes, that he cried "murder," and that the aum—; ence in a body came rushing over the stage to see was the matter. I -left the town early the mist lug, and remained on the Continent for three reen,'O until I felt that I could a little better bear to face 0' friends.—London Society Christmas Number.

OVER THE SUNSHINE OF EXISFENEE HANGS A BLACK CLOUD. Wits the uncertainty of life Is miugled the dark mystery death! The promptings of instinct are but the spontalse°:, voices of nature, and it is our duty to obey. But there 13 sod remains the question, can death be postponed by a single boor, Yes; for the world works in o'vdienee to certain laws; study of these proves that those who have the judgment the will to buckle on the shield, which nature places reasli '- their grasp. may ward off the insidious attacks of the IMPIller,„„ able enemy of life, until, in a rips old age, the vital faculf7r gradually decay, and the Angel of Peace glides softly Int° °tile preser ea, leading us, a, it were, in a gentle slumber to regions bey iscl the shadow of the tomb.

General Lord Wolseley telegraphs :—" Korti, Sunday, 330 P.m.—Letters from Brigadier Stewart, from Hambolr, Where he leaves a post to improve water supply. He will be here about noon to-morrow. Has left the Guards' regi- Ment at liakdal, 100 miles from Korti, strongly fortified in impregnable position, with plenty of good water and pro- visions. He picked up a few of the Mandi's men as pri- sonera. His march was a complete surprise to the Arabs in the desert. He writes in the highest possible praise of the ...way all ranks worked. Not a sick man in his column. xeeterday Stafford Rpgiment rowed safely .up so-called Cataract of Gerenciid, and are now campeil at liamdab.!Will soon have force there ready for advance into, Mouasir. coon. UV. All going on well." GAIEDUL WELLS (VIA KOKTI), SUNDAY, 4 P.m —Genera( 8, tewart's force, with its convoy of supplies, has arrived nere. The journey of 07 miles was accomplished in 65 lumrs, and during that time the camels were not once Watered. The road lead over many rough places, where Marching was very difficult. The force left Korti on Toes. day afternoon at three o'clock, and did not bivouac' until eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, when Abu Nefki was reached. Here there was some excitement, owing to the . . _ .

Uncertainty as to the inhabitants. Only a few huts were Visible, and these were deserted. Plenty of green Udder was Obtainable. The troops remained on the spot quite undis- turbed, until three in the afternoon, when a start was again Made. Both men and animals were greatly refreshed by the rest, and the men all seemed to vie with each other in the smartness with which they remounted when the order Was given. The formation observed almost throughout the "s'iltlarch was column of companies, and the force was so ;distributed that in two minutes three squares could be ~ formed in echelon to resist any attack. All the men are , Jail of excitement. There are conflicting reports as to ; hether our possession of the wells will be contested by the ' 111e°13% Everything is being done to make our position se- ' are. General Stewart returns without delay to Korti. . . e supply of water is unlimited. The troops reached the rat wells, called Lesheen, on W ednesday evening, but the ' -W, &ter Supply being scarce they moved on almost immediate- I:: ' :IY. The new year was ushered in with great cheering from tile men, which rang far aid wide over the plains, and echoed thrott4h the hills. Hardly had the cheering ceased when 'there was again a cry of "Wells ahead" Thia instantly l'rought the 261 h Company of Royal Engineers to the front, and, under the direction of Maier Doward, the tripod pumps soon supplied the men's wants. On Thursday morning at tight o'clock the men mounted to continue their merch to tile Gadkul Wells, capturing on their way a qnantity of spoil and making all the natives they met prisoners. Captain 'Panshaws, with a troop of the 19th Hussars, succeeded in ' 'capturing a prominent sheikh, named Abn Loola, toeether ith hie family. The Mudir of Dongala once offered a neusand dollars for the sheikh's head. On Thursday eight edajorKitchener, with an escert, captured five natives from t 4 but, who are acid to have been the Mahrli's meat contrac- :". Gedkul Wells were secured on Friday morning at ''eVen o'clock. The natives had all disappeared. The water slas found to be good. A movable hospital accompanied the force under Surgeon Sages. Five more natives were Ptured and brought in by Captain Waleh's division of saounted Infantry. Two of them wore the Mandi's uniform, 1:11.1d all attempted to evade capture, being well armed and elaposed to fight. The force, marching in extended order, 'oYerea a frontage of 40 yards, with scouts as the advance t,o‘d rear guards, and presented a most formidable appearance. :ace natives state that the Mandi's force is terrified, declar- 41g that there is no end to the British troops. TONQUIN.--FRUNCLI VICTORIES. Pews, SurrnKr.—An official despatch from Hanoi states that General Negrier yesterday defeated a body of 6,000 Chinese at a place one day's journey east of Chu. No further details are given. - • PARIS, MONDAY.—A telegram ' from Hanoi states that after their defeat to the eastward of Chu, the Chinese troops, to the number of 12,000, returned to take the offen- olive. General Negrier, thereupon attacked them, and suc- ceeded in penetrating into their positions, which were de- fended by forts with rows of batteries one above the other. The Chinese were repulsed and completely routed after an Aive resistance, abandoning all their positions. Two bat- teries of Krupp guns' a quantity of rifles, ammunition, and provisions, tegetber with the Chinese etandards and convoys fell into the hands of the French. On the Chinese side there were 600 killed and a considerable number wounded. The French loss in both engagements consisted of three officers slightly wounded, 18 men killed, and 65 wounded.'

The Standard correspondent at Tainat eve telegraphs that the French, aided by a force of Sakalvae, had attacked the Howie in their positions near the town of Vohemar. The French report that they killed 250 Hovas and took a few prisoners. Two guns are alsolsaid to have been captured. The French state that there are now no liovas anywhere on the coast between Cape Amber and Amboanio, and think that the effect of this victory may be to terrify the Hones into an acceptance of their demands. Everything is quiet at Tamatave and at the capital. THE UNITED STATES.—EARTHQUAKE. NEW YORE, SATURDAY.-9. shock supposed to be due to an earth:lll'llre *as felt yesterday evening in the southern section of Frederick County, Maryland. Persons in New Hampshire and Washington and its vicinity assert that they also felt the shock. REPORTED DISCOVERY OF A DYNAMITARDJ

_ SOCIETY. NEW YORE. TECIIISDAY.—Romours are current in West- moreland County, Pennsylvania, that English detectives have obtained evidence that a powerful society of Dynami- tards exists in that county, which is directly responsible for the recent expluaions and outrages in England. It is added that the ' detectives hive gone to Washington in order to inform the Hon.- Sackville West, British Minister, of their discovery. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT BUENOS AYRES. BUENOS AYESS, MONDAY.—A railway accident has occur- red on the Southern Railway. Twenty persons were killed or injured' THE NICARAGUA CANAL SCHEME. Weswrstavrotv, TEZESDAY.—The Foreign Affairs Com- mittee of the Senate have reported in favour of ratifying the treaty with Nicaragua.
