ARRINGTON TRUE BLUES (2Na TEAM) V. Sr. BARNABAS (IST TEAM).—A match was played betwem the above cubs on the grmand of the former, and resulted in an easy win for the home team. Score :—One goal, eight tries, nine minor points, to nil. EARLEsTOWN (2ND TEAM) V. EARLESTONVN RAMBLERS (IsT).—Tbis match was played on the ground of the first- named at Wargrave Moss, on New Year's Day, in the presence of a fair number of speatators. The borne team played with nne :nen, bat succeeded in winning by two goals to one. RUNCORN Sr. JOHN'S JUNIORS V. MERSEY MISSIONS 2een.—A match between these two clubs was played on the ground of the last named on Saturday, ending in a victory for the Juniors by 1 goal and 6 minor points, to 1 try and 2 minor points. Good play VMS made for the Juniors by Mareb, Leach, Brockley, and Houghton, and for the Mission by Jones and Shaw. NICHOL-LANE (ASHTON) FOOTEVALL Cern t football match was played between Ashton Recreation 2nd eleven and Nichol-lane 2nd eleven, on New Year's Day. The snore was Nichol-lane four goale, and Ashton Recreation two goals. A match was played on Saturday between Nichol-lane Ist team and Stubehaw Cross Ist team. Nichol- lane scored seven goals, and Stubsbaw Cross one goal. Both matches were played on the Nichol-lane ground. • NEW SPRINGS V. EARLESTOWN ROVERS (2ND TEAMS.)— This return match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and was looked forward to with much interest, especially as the first match on the Eirlestown ground Was won by the home team after a very even game by one goal to nil. The home team were pretty confident of being able to reverse the first result, which proved to be the case, the Rovers being the losers by four goals to one. EARLESTOWN (21S.'D TEAM) V. HANDOCE RECREATION (IST). these teams met at Wargrave Moss on the afternoon of New Year's Day. There was a good attendance of spec- tators. The home team were aseisted by Sims and Dux- bury, of the first eleven, and playing up hill in the first half they scored four goals to none. On the change ot ends the play became of a more even character, but the Earles- toniana had the best of the game, and ultimately icon by six goals to one. R „ e , e Te; UNCORN A RECREATION V. IREDALE EA3li. ...I match was played on the Recreation ground on New Year's Day. The bill being started by the Recreation captain, was kept in neutral ground for some time, when the Recrea- tion by a senate bit of play rushed the ball up to their op- ponents' line, which Faulkner nicely cleated, gaining a try for the Recreation, the kick at goal failing. Half -time soon was celled, the ball was again set rolling, and the Recreation soon obtained a touch-in-goal. Play was kept uo in the Kirkdale 25, but only to obtain minor points. On call of time the Recreation was left winners by one try and four minor points to WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION (A. TEAM) V. MANCHESTER CLIFFORD (ATEA/O.—This very pleasant match was played at Old Trafford on Saturday, and resulted in an easy win for the visitors,Clifford, having to provide two A teams were considerably over-matched, and were beaten by three goals and one disputed to nil. The goals were kicked by E. Dillon (2), Webster, and Siddall (disputed). Teams :—Clifford: Goal, Wright; backs, Houston and Bebbington; half-backs, Kershaw, Jenkins, and D. Houston; forwards, Thompson, Barber, Ryder, Chadwick, and Hutchinson. Warrington : Goal, B. Parker; backs, Royston and Pearson; half-backs, Jones, Walton, and E. Parker; forwards, Allen, Siddall, E. 11 Dillon, Matthews, and Webster. HAvDCCH TEMPERANCE (IST) V. EARLESTOWN (2ND).—A match between the Ist team of the Haydock Temperance and Earlestown Clubs bad been arranged to be played on the ground of the last-named at Wargrave Moss, Etrles- town, on Friday afternoon, but owing to the Earlestown club having to play a Liverpool and District Challenge Cup tie on the following day (Saturday), the committee at the last moment thought it better to place their second team in the field to oppose the Haydock representatives. J. Green, however, rendered them great assistance. A large number of persons assembled to witness the match, which resulted in a draw of two goals each. The following were the players :—Haydeek Temperance: W. Knowles, goal; Hatton and Carter, backs; Plant, Ellie, and flame. half-backs; Blackie and, Taylor, right wing; Briscoe and BarriSoo, left wing; Twist, centre; umpire, Mr. G. H. Hunt. Earleotown: J. Harrison, goal ; J. Green and C. Emmett, backs; A. Clayton and J. Gray, half .backs; IL Holcroft and J. Apple- ton, right wing; T. Ferguson and W. Murray, left wing; W. Thompson and J. James, centre; umpire, Mr. T. Bell. LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT CHALLENGE Cup: EARLES. TOWN V. SKELMERSDALE.—ConsiderabIe interest centered in the meeting of the Earlestown and Skelmersdale clubs in tho third round of the competition for the Liverpool and District Association Challenge Cup, at Earlestown on Sat- urday afternoon. As the Skelmersdale team have lately displayed good form aud as the Earlestown team is generally supposed to have a good chtnce of winning the cap ebbe season, for which they were the "runners-Up "in the last competition, about 500 spectators assembled to witness the game, a goodly number of supporters having accompanied the Skelrnersdale representatives, The teams appeared on the field shortly after half-past two, and the visitors hav- ing won the toss chose toPlay down hill in the first half. The Earlestonians started the leather, and for a short time kept it in the Skelmersdale quarters. The visitors, however, quickly assumed the aggressive, and playing with great spirit, pressed the Silver Medallists. The attack of the visitors was kept up for about 15 minutes, after which the Etrlestonians gradually wore their opponents down by superior play and tactics. Before half-time Etrlestown scored three goals amid load cheers from their supporters, and ends were changed before the Skelmersdale players had notched a single point. On the change of ends the home tram had matters pretty much their own way, and very severely pressed their opponents. When time was called the Earlestown team retired the victors by five goals to none. The Earlestown team was as follows : J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and J. Green, backs ; J. Whalley. J. Duxbury, and R. Bowker, half-backs; J. Sims and J. Ogden, left wing ; A. W. Daguall. centre ; W. Rich and J. Ellison, right wing. The referee was Mr. R. E. Lyth- goe, secretary Liverpool and District Association.

NOTES BY THE WAY. Owing to the frost on Saturday many fixtures were aban- doned, much to the disappointment of football followers. But in Lancashire and Yorkshire most of the contests were brought to an issue. Several well-known Scotch teams have tried conclusions with Lanc.shire combinations, who have generally hada decided pull over their opponents, and on Saturday the first international contest of the season was brought to an issue at Swansea, when England obtained a substantial victory over Wales. The game was wit- nessed by a vast concourse of spectators. In addition to ties in the National Cup competition, the following matches were played en Saturday :—ln the Lon- don Cup competition the Old Etonian, (ten men) and Dul. wich again played drawn game, three goals each; Old

Foresters beat Barnes by three to none. In the Wake and Border Counties Cup competition, the Druids beat Gnirk by two goals to none. The 3;cl Lanark beat Wed n-sbury. at Wedneebury, by one to none; at Newcastl., L.narksbire beat Northumberland by five to none; Dumhartun and Warsall Swifts played a drawn game, one goal each, at War. sail ; Derby County beat Waaaall, at Derby, by one to none ; the Vale of Leven and Thotnliebank played drawn game without scoring, at Alexandria ; Hurlfor beat Kul- marnock by two goals to none; Glasgow Thistle beat Arbroath, at Arbroath, by five to three ; Renton, at Dundee, beat Harp by five to two ; Strathmore and Patrick Thistle played a drawn game, one goal each; Nott Rangers and Derby Midland played a drawn game, one goal each, at Darby ; the Old Foresters beat Clapham Rovers by three goals to none; at Bolton, the Wanderers beat St. Bernard's (Edinburgh) by seven to none ; Astley Bridge beat Cam- buslang by tire to none; Great Lever beat Pollokshields Athletic by six to none; Hilliwell and Kilmarnock played a drawn game, one each; Port Glasgow Athletic beat Tyre by five to none.
GENER AL NEWS.

The steel works of Messrs. Bolckow, Vaughan, and Co., at Eaton, which were closed about ten days age, resumed work on Monday A Windsor correspondent says it is expected that the marriage of the Princess Beatrice will take place about the middle of April Mr. William Fair, a well-known agriculturist, of Great Budworth, Cheehire, was thrown eut of his trap on Fri- day night and killed. The deceased was a remarkably heavy men. The man Fennelly, arrested at Dudley on suspicion of being concerned in the recent dynamite explosions, has been liberated, as a satisfactory account of his recent movements leaf! forthcoming. Mr. Parnell delivered a speech in Tipperary on Thursday, in which he announced a new agitation against the present "'fair rents," and predicted that the time was rapidly ap- proaching when an Irish Parliament would assemble in Dublin. At Portsnaonth, on Saturday, a joiner named Hill, em- ployed in the Portsmouth Dockyard, was charged with ' stealing £478 from a secret drawer which he had made for a neighbour. The prisoner's defence was that he' had saved the money from his earnings. He was thee' charged. CATFLE PLAGUE IN IRELAND —Fcom the south of Ireland an outbreak of a very virulent disease among cattle is re- ported. A large number of cattle have aleeadv succumbed to whit is known as "Black quarter," a destructive aid practically iucurable inelady. It was thought not to be in- fections, but the rapidity with which it his spread has shaken the fanners' belief. The owners of made are adopt- ing every precaution ,againet the contagion. THE PENISTONE COLLISION: A FOURTH Dnaaes.—Another death occurred on Saturday in the Sheffield Infirmary as the result of the railway collision near Penistoae, the deceesed being Mr. William Harrison, wood turner, of Sheffield. The Board of Trade inquiry into the cause of the disaster was opened at Penistone Station on Saturday, and, after some evidence had been taken, was adjourned to Manches- ter. Only formal evidence has yet been taken at the in- quests. ANOTHER FATAL Ices ACCIDENT.—At Betley Court, near Crewe, on Saturday, three young um- ventured upon a pond that was much shaded by a plantation, and ths ice, bong only half an inch thick, gave way. One scrembled out, another was neve: seen again, and the thiali after clinging •to the ice which time after time broke in his grasp, disappeared alter half-an-hour's agonising effert in the presence of his fathetein-law andeother spectators, and was drowned. Mn. Ham GEORGE WI REYE.—Mr. Henry George ad- dressed a meeting of the inhabitants of Portfree on Monday evening, the chair being occupied by the Rev. Mr. Mclntyre, UT. Church. Mr. George made special allu- sion to the present condition of the crofters in Skyey and urged his audience to bestir themselves in behalf of their rights. The speaker was frequently cheered. Earlier in the day Mr. George addressed a meeting of crofMrs at Broadford. PUBLIC SANITARY InsPacrons' ASSOCILTION.—A meting WAS held in London on Saturday, at which Mr. E. C. Deebins read a paper on the growing importance and responsibility of public sanitary inspectors. He contended that the posi- tion of the public sanitary inspector had not improved in - proportion to its importance and responsibility, and should be made more independent of the local authority. The in- spectors, he thought, should be willing to submit themselves for examination to some recognised sanitary authority, whose certificite would have a distinct money value as a testimonial meritoriously acquired. SIR C. DILKE AS A RARICAL CANDIDATE.—WrSing to members of the Liberal organisation in the berough of Chelsea, on the subject of his condidature under the altered condition envied by the redistribution of seats, Sir Charles Dilke signifies his willingness to stand for the sizepolliag districts forming his native parish af Chelsea. The right hon. baronet also exiireeseevahis belief that he will ha able to speak with a force which is greater and beyond any per- sonal strength, and which will excuse any personal weak- ness, as a representative of advanced or Radical opinion, if be is returned to Parliament by one of the more advauced or Radical parts of the present borough. Lome It. GROSVENOR. ON PROTECTION.—Lorti Richard Grosvenor. M.P., addressing his constituents at Caergwrle, near Wrexham, on Monday night, reviewed the efforte made by the Liberal party to.eecure the passage of tha Franchise Bill, and then proceeded to speak upon tee trade depression existing throughout th. country. The Tories once more once bringing forward their pet doll Protection which they attempted to disguise in various dresses, but It Was still the same thing after all. There was depression in various trades all over the country no doubt but it was due to over pro- duction and not to Free Trade. This would, however, be best cured by natural c mess. The noble lord quoted statistics •to show that the trade was more depressed in protected countries like France and America than, La England, and in conclusion expressed the opinion that one of the most im- portant duties of the new Parliament would be to amend the rules governing its proceedings. FALL cnr. a Carmen GALLERY.—An accident which re- sulted fatally to one lady and injuries more or less serious to several other persons, occurred oa Sunday evening at this Presbyterian Church, Gloucester-road, London, during divine _ service. The officiating minister, the Rev. G. Watsone bad scarcely commenced his disconrse, when a small gallery, which bad only recently been erected, after giving several preliminary signs of insecurity, suddenly gave way, preci- pitating its occupants to the ground. Medical assistance was summoned, and an examination showed that Miss MlR- land, an elderly maiden lady, residing close to the church, was deed, she having sustained a severe scalp wound and other injwries. Five or six other persons had sustained in. juries, the most serious case being that of a young man who had an arm and a leg broken. The cause of the gallery falling is said to be the we aleoese of a beam upon which it principally rested. The gallery was crowded at the time the accident happened. DEATH OF TIIE BISHOP OF LONDON.—WO regret to an- nounce the death of Dr. Jackson, the Bishop of London, which occurred early on Tuesday morning in the Palace at Fulham. The clergy at St. Paul's received intimation of the sad event at a comparatively. early hour on Tuesday morning. The "Dead March in Saul "was played on the organ at the conclusion of the ordinary morning service, but no allusion was made to the Bishop's death. It was known at the Cathedral that his lordship had been in en- feebled health for some time, but no change for the worse was noticed when he preached on Sunday evening, although his voice seemed more feeble. Daring the disturbance in the Cathedral on that occasion, caused by a fanatic named Freund, his lordship remained standing in his pulpit, and after the offender had been ejected went on with his ser- mon without displaying any agitation. His lordship ap- pears for some time to have entertained the belief that he should not live long, and expressed this opinion at a recent viaitation. Ile expired in his bed at half-past three o'clock on Tuesday morning. The immediate CIUSS of the Bishop of London's death was heart disease. Mn. CH&NBERLSIN AT ButuninnAll.—Mr. Chamberlain was entertained at dinner on Monday evening by the Birm- ingham Artisans' Association. In responding to the toast of his health he made a short speech, in which he taunted the local Conservatives on the result of the charges brought against himself and the "Caucus" in connection with the Alen Park disturbance. Afterwards, he spoke in acknowe ment of a resolution which congratulated him on the passing of the Franchise Bill and on the prospects of the Seats Bill. The right hon. gentlemen, referring to the change which had come over political affairs since he last addressed a public meeting said that the 'Liberal party now found themselves in full possesion of the fruits of victory without having fired a shot or drawn a sword. In fact, all parties seemed to be contented, and the general felicity was only broken by the plaintive mariners of the members of the Society for Proportional Representation. He congratulated his audience on the passing of the Franchise Bill, and the prospect of the speedy passing of the Redistribution Bill. If the present Redistribution Bill did not become law, he warned the Conservatives that it would be replaced by still more sweeping measures. In view of the chaeges brought about by the Reform Bills, he advised the formation of district Liberal councils, who shetild alone be responsible for the selection of candidates. The aggregate of the committees would form a united Liberal body to define and formulate the programme of the Liberal party. The extension of popular authority, would, he be- lieved, make for peace. lie thought democracy would have no love for a policy of intervention and aggression. The people would lend no assistance to those who clamoured in the interests of the bondholders for us to take possession of Egypt. Our task there had proved greater than anticipated, but the Government would not be driven from their inten- tions. The right hon. gentleman maintained that if the occasion should arise to assert the authority of England a democratic Government would know how to make itself re- spected, and said be considered the spirit of uneasiness dis- played by Some politicians absolutely inconsistent with the dignity of a great nation. He then referred to the colonial policy of Germany, and sail it might be neceesery to review our foreign and colonial policy in the light of recent events, but if it was necessary let us do this in the spirit of full- gthroe wane t imo ne n taanide nn obty atsh ef r Gi g ehrtme na end Government el dr nr emn .9 n tie, we hr jecghr e thteadd already produced the deepest irritation and alarm in the great aependencies of the English Crown. div.p: TTIE EXAMINER. SA TIJRDAY. JANUARY 10, 1885.
PENKPIIII MUTUAL IMPROVENIENT;

ASSOCIATION. The third acnual conversazione of the l'enketh Mutual Improyetmnt Association was given by the President last evening week in the Elementary Schoolroom, which had been most tas'efully and appropriately decorated .for the occasion by some of the more active members. Several pictures bad been lent, and adorned the walls of the room, and there were exhibited a number of interesting fossils lent by Mr Tonga, a variety of samples showing the pro- cess of iron making lent by Mr Morris, an excellently arranged set of samples il'ustratlye of the manufacture Of cotton from the raw material to the finished cloth presented by Mr C Marshall (of Bolton), several interesting curiosi- ties shown by Mr Madeley (of the Warrington Museum and Library), and various other articles of interest exhibited by members and friends of the Association in Peuketh. The proceedings commenced at seven o'clock, at which ' heur there were present, amongst others—The President (Mr J Dodds) and Mrs Dodds, Hey J and Mrs McTurk, Rev , aFnd MGsrs Cutting,(of B Rene)y Miss ilsis aFncilt tonrs (JDo Mn,iessmMryr )J. -rmorn Fitton (Runcorn), Mrs J J Steckdale (Stockport). Min Maud Lomax (Stockport), Mrs Jenks (Lou. don), Mr Thomas Morris, F 0 S, Mrs Morris. Miss Weldon, Mies Wallington, Mr T R Ford, Mr C Madeley, and Mr Frederick Wright (Warrington), Mr and Mrs Edward Walker (Liverpool), Mr Arthur Bennett (Padgate), Mr Robert Garnett and Miss Garnett, Misses Moses, Mr W Craven (Sheffield), Mr D Garnett, Mr Sidney Garnett, br J H Crarnall, Mrs Gorsall, Mr J 1.1 Gornall, :unior, Mr C E Parker (secretary), Miss Parker, Mr and Mr a J Wat- son, Mr and Mrs J Maialey, Mr and Mr.; A J White, lir and Mrs 0 Coak, Mr T Davies, Mr F Davies, Miss Davies, Mr Longehaw, Mr H Hughes, Mr Frank Hughes. Mr Fred Hughes, Mr J Routledge and the Misses Routledge, C George, Mr E Cross, Mr Haokinson, Mr and Mrs E Rankin- son, Mr Baxter, Mr and Mrs Seed, Mr and Mm Wilson, Mr and Mrs Randall, Mr and Min Atbedon, Mr and Mrs Moores, Mr G Parker, Mr P Johnson, Mr Gandy, Mr Tetlow, Miss Griffiths, Mr W Hooper, Mr T Bell, Mr Cunliffe, Mr D Dobson, Mrs Plumpton, Miss Plimpton, Mrs Soderland, Miss Sullen. Miss Seed, Miss Neil!, Mr J Dumbill, Mr Fodett) Mr A Greenlaalgb, Mr li Dale, etc. The proceedings were opened by the singiag of a well known hymn. After prayer had been offered by the Rev.J. McTurk, the president, in a few appropriate sentences, bade the company heartily welcome. He said they would observe from the programme that he was erepeeed to give an intro- ductory address. (Applause.) He did not intend to do so, inasmuch as the programme centained, as they would see, the names cf ladies and gentlemen who bad come from a die. tance specially prepared to occupy the very limited time at their disposal, and he had such frequent opportunities of addressing them at their ordinary meetings. Farther, there- fore than to atate that the association had so far beam a complete success, was a happy family, united and therefore strong, every member devoting time and ability in sustaining and developing its work, be would not longer stand between them and the good things to follow. (Applause.)—Miss A. Moses then sang "The Merchant of Cheapside ' is a way which won much applause —Mr. Wats in next gave an address on "Cotton." He explained that cotton of cammerce was really a kind of hairy appendage or covering of the seed of the cotton plant, and if magnified it would have something of the appearance of a comer, sad the seed of the cotton represantZng the nucleus of the comet, and the hairy appendage the tail. Having referred to tee mode of cultivatioa, be said the plant was subject to many dangers, as one night's frost would blast the whole crop and one day's cold north-east wind would do the same. There were also various insects which nibbled the plant, and to- wards autumn particularly a kind of caterpillar appeared which deposited its, eggs upon the leaves of the plant. In a few hours these eggs were hatched, and in about ten days a little insect began.to eat the leaves, and a cotton field 400 acres in extent had been destroyed in four days by means of these ravenouelittlepreatures. The cotton having been picked it was placed in bags and taken into the drying rooms, and afterwards it was " ecatched " or pickect that was to say that seeds, and leaves, atones, &a, were taken from amongst it. The packing in bags for exportation was done by hydraulicsmachinery, by the-pressure of which a large quantity of cotton could be compressed into a small space. In England there were different kinds of machinery for the manufacture of different kinds of cotton, a special kind of machinery being used for the manufacture of the better kind of cotton. In the mills the cotton was passed through blowing or scutching machines by which it was, so to speak, torn. iota shreds, and a drying current of air passed through it, and the dust blown (Alt of it. From the blowing machine it was passed on to the carding machine, by which-it was separated into fine layers, and the fibres were placed as nearly as pos- sible parallel with each other. This work of clearing and carding the cotton was formerly, Mr. Watson explained, done by women and children, bet was new done by machinery. He then referred to various inventions by which the manufacture of cotton cloth had been facilitated and improved., and by means of samples of cotton material In various stages of manufacture he explained the process through which the material had to go before it was placed in the handaof the consumer, and concluded a brief but in- teresting address amidst applause.—. Mr. T. R. Ford then executed an excellent solo on the harp, after which Mr. C. E. Parker gave a short account of the manner in which leather is produced, his remarks being also illustrated by specimens of different kinds of leather,, and the herbs, dm., which aid in the production of the saleable conoraodity.—A song having been sung by Miss Wallington and very heartily applauded, Mr. Tongs, C.E., F.G.S., gave an address on "Coal." He said that coal, iron, and cotton, thsee subjects which were to be spoken on that night, were without doubt of the greatest interest to Lancashire. (Hear, hear.) He might just mention in passing that the coal measures yielded perhaps a large) ameunt of iron than any other measure in the earth's atrata, so that coal and iron were not on/y very closely connected in their manufactures, but also in the earth's crust. It seemed to be intended that they should always go together. (Ilear„hear.) Those who had not etudied the matter would be wondering what coal really was. The great George Stephenson called it "bottled sun- light," and he (Ms. Tooge) thought that was perhaps in a few words nearer to the truth than any other form of ex- pression. (Applause.) The geologists divided the time of the formation of the earth's crust into four periods. They formerly had another age called the dead age, that WAS the age when there was no life on the earth, but like many other sciencoa geology taught them to be careful in what they said so that now instead of saying the age of no life they say the age in which no signs of life have been found. It was in the mast recent parts of the palaeozeic age—in the carboniferous formations—teat the great deposits of coal

were found. The earth was once molten and. began grad- ually to cool until it got to that condition in which plant- life could exist and did exist most abundantly, there being in tact a temperature more genial than bad ever before ex- isted or ever had sines. Almost all the coal they got either in Great Britain or in any other country was formed during this very limited period of the carboniferous age. If they examined coal by the aid of the microscope they found that it was formed precisely like our present vegetable life. and if they examined it chemically they found it contained the some chemioal elements. (Applause.) From the way the coal is surrounded by other matter they saw that dar- ing the age it was being formed the earth was in a very lively state. It was very hot and there was very extensive con- vulsions; there were also a series of elevations and depressions. so that they found that coal, instead of being in one great bed, the undisturbed growth of many hundreds of millions of years. had been gradually raised and depressed, thus allowing of alternate layers of sandstone and other material. They therefore now found coal at various depths, coming up to the surface of the earth in some parts, and in others they had mines going down to rather over half a mile. It had to be brought from this great depth because of the upper portions having been taken away so rapidly. There was some talk about their coal supply coming to an end, and Sir William Armstrong frightened some people by saying that that would be in another hundred years, but he (Mr. Tonge) did not think any of them need be afrkid of that, as it would probably last a thousand instead of a hundred years. (Loud applause.)—The song," At the ferry," was then very prettily rendered by Miss Garnett.—The next address was by lAr, T. Morris, his subject being " Iron." Having said that in speaking about iron he would take his text from the first book of granite, he went on to explain the origin and nature of iron, making use for the purposes of illustration of a number of interesting and valuable specimen', and of a diagram which he had brought for the purpose. Mt. Morris also gave an instructive description of the processes of the manufacture cf iron, and he mentioned as an illustration of the improveroonts intro- duced in late years, that twenty-five years ago it took three men and two lads about a day to make a dozen iron buckets, but recently he had seen one man and a few lads making buckets by machinery at the rate of 240 in ten hours. In concluding, he said, amidst applause, that some other time he should be glad to give them a lecture on the subject.— . The Union Jack "was then sung by Mr. P. Johnson.—Mr. Madeley gave a short address on 301110 local" Exhibits from the Warrington Museum." He said he had bronght with him to show them, and ask them a few questions about, some specimens of Penketh literature for the last 400 years. tie had got the letters of William Thompson, who was a Quaker schoolmaster at Penketh 70 years ago. They had also a rather interesting manuscript letter of his on epistol- ary style, and he (Mr. Madeley) should like to know if any. one could tell him to whom the letter was addressed. Going back 200 years they came to another Quaker, Roger Had- dock, of whose works he had got a collection, and to Peter Slinehead. If they went back other 200 years—for Pen- keth literature seemed only to flourish at intervals of 200 years—they had got in the Museum a book dated 1474, a book edited by a Penketh man. He could not tell what it was about, as he could not read it, nor had he been able to find anybody who could. (Laughter.) It was one of the books of Dons Septus, and it was edited by Thomas Penketh. Thomas Penketh was the son of the Squire of Penketh of those days. lie joined the Augustan friary at Warrington bridge, went to Oxford and took his degree, and then went to Italy and was made professor at the University of Padua. He there edited the works of Duna Scottie, and afterwards came back to England and was made provincial of the Augustan friars in London. lie was the only Pen- keth man mentioned by Shakespeare, and they would find reference to him, he (Mr. Madeley) believed, in the play of Richard 111. (Applause.) Mr. Madeley then exhibited some other.curiosities from the Museum, such as thumb- screws, a brank or scold's bridle, &c.—A duet, " Oh, wer't thou in the cauld blast," having been excellently sung by the Misses Moses, and grace sung by the company, suitable refreshments were served round.—The second part of the

trogramme was introduced by a short address by the Rev. J. Merolla, in which he referred to the good work done by associations of that kind. He was glad. he eaid, to find that they had ladies in that Association. (Applause.) If Eng. land was to retain her present poeition, if she was not only to be mistress of the seas, but also heed of a great empire, she must have in this country intelligent educated people, a people with en- lightened intellects, with deep convictions, and who were able to give expression to those convictions, for,an England without these would c,rtainly not be able to hold her own among the nations of the world. (Hear, hear, and ap- planse.)—.Mrs.Dadds, who was received with prolonged ap- plause, next sung in an expressive manner Tennyson, emg, ' Ring out, wild bells," after which and a harp solo by far.,, Ford. part of the trial scene In "The Merchant of Venice" was very creditably performed, the two principal parts of. Portia and Shylock being taken by Miss F. Garnett and Mr. Hobson respectively.—The President then proposed a votes( thanks to the speakers and singers who had come from a, distance.—This was seconded by Mr. Craven, and supported by the Rev. G. E. Cutting, and carried by acclamation.—Mr. Garnett said it would not be due te themselves if they separated without expressing their feelings and thanks in as substantial a way as they were able to do to their esteemed' president and his wife. (Loud applauss.) Personally he felt very much obliged to Mr Dodds and his good lady, and he was quite sure he uttered all their feelings when he wished Mr. and Mrs. Dodds and their children dong life and hap- piness, mad that the year just begun might be a healthy and prosperous year to them. (Loud applause.) Mr. Dodds had almost out-done himself in the way he had catered for their enjoyment that evening. He had left nothing undone, and, in fee, he had made it rather hot for any president who might come after him, but they bad made up their minds that Mr. Dodds should be president for ever. (Laugh-, ter and applause.)—Mr. White seconded this vote of thanks which was carried by prolonged aeclamation.—.Mr.Docidei in briefly responding on behalf of himself and his wife, said he couhl not tell them how pleased he was with the success which bad attended the Mutual Improvement Association of Penketh. It had been beyond what he ever anticipated, and in the future he sheuld always be willing to do what he could to sustain it and to further its interests. (Applause.) He had met many friends in Penketh—friends whom he should never forget. Through whatever vicissitudes he might pass he should always look back with pleasure on the connection he had with the workingmm of Penketh. (Loud applause,) —As cordial vote of thanks was next given on the motion of Mr. Hobson, to the secretary, Mr. Parker, soon after which a most enjoyable gathering wan brought to a close.

At the usual weekly meeting of the society, held on Wednesday evening, last, in the Day School, and before a large attendance of the members, Mr. James Watson in the chair, an excellent paper on " Oliver Cromwell" was read by Mr. W. Longshaw, who gave a succinct account of the great Commoner's career. An interesting discussion fol- lowed. The president glanced at the times in which Cro- mwell lived, and dealt with his character and work, and while holding that his motives were of the noblest kind, and his work on the whole worthy of every praise, con- demned his treatment of his parliament, and his action in levying taxes withEut consultation with them during his protectorate, as being in themselves and apart from moti.res, almost as Irregular and blameworthy as the similar doings of Charles the First. He attributed the great success of Cromwell's " Tronside'a" in battle to the high moral and religious training and character of the men and to their faith in the justice of their cause and in God.—Mr. A. J. White, Mr. C. E. Parker, Mr. Pownall, the Chairman, and others having taken part, the usual vote of thanks was passed and the meeting closed.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL –
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL -

The monthly meeting of this body was held in the Coun- cil Chamber at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), presiding. There were also present Aldermen Burgess, Davies, Holmes, Chandley, and Kean ; Councillors Broadbent, Litton, Hutchinson, Green- ing, Fleming. Roberts, Francomb, Dixon, Dakio, Burgess. Bolton, Mackie, Ashton. Marsh, Milner, W, Pierpoint, J. Pierpoint, Sutton,-Whlttle, Tinsley, Crosfield and Wright; W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough sur- veyor), and .1. 11. Gornall (medical officer.) SANITARY cosrarrrxx.—COMPULSOßY, NOTIFICATION OP MEASLES AND WHOOPING COUGH. _ _ . . _

Alderman BURGESS moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee. There was one important matter regarding which it was absolutely necessary that he shordd ask the serious attention of the Council. That was a recommenda- tion that application be made to the lecal Government Board for sanction to include measles and whooping cough with those diseases in regard to which notification was made compulsory. The result of their experience as a Corpora- tion, was that, having obtained in 1879 Dowere for the noti- fication of specreed diseases, they bad hail an immunity to an extent not previously experienced of such diseases. Whilst they were congratulating them- selves that scarlet fever had „scarcely shown itself in the borouvh in the past year, and while in the first quarter of the year there was such a lew death rate as to be almost remarkable, they were overtaken be an infections disease of a lamentable character. For the first quarter of 1884 the death rate was 181 per 1,000; for the second quarter it was 159 per I,oooi About that period the epidemic referred to set in, and they would at once see the result In the third quarter the death rate was 23 4 per 1,000, and in the fourth, ending December last, it was 27.8 oer 1,000. They had a mortality within the last six months from measles alone ef no less than 100 persons, and the death rite for the whole year was 21.3 per 1,000. That rate was in reality satisfac- tory, but how mach more satisfactory might it not have been but for the 100 deaths from measles. While they had hospital accommodation and requirements scircely to be surpassed in the kingdom, and a sufficient staff for conduct- ing it, he believed that he was correct in saying that at that moment there was only one occupant. They thought as a cemmittee, and thought that the Council would agree with them, that the time was now come when they might with perfect propriety ask the Council to join them in asking the Local Government Board for an extension of the clause rendering notification compulsory to measles and whooping cough. The Local Board of Hiydock had applied for use of the hospital and terms, but the experience the commit- tee had had did not level them to entertain the proposal. People had need them for their own convenience, and like a sucked orange, thrown. them away when they had got what advantage they could. Therefore they had respect- fully declined to entertain the application. With regard to the number of tenders that were recommended for adoption, and which were for machinery, plant, building, and works required in connectien with the Longford scheme, Alder- man Burgess said that they, if passed, were subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. The tenders, he added, bad besn chosen with a desire to promote the best interests of the borough. The last recommendation, that ap- plication be made for permission to borrow a stun not ex- ceeding £12,000 for the purpose of completing the night soil depot and introducing a better method of collection and removal of refuse required 801110 explanation. Mr. Long. din's report said that £9,133 would be required for the com- pletion of the work. and the introduction of the new mode of collecting the night soil with the intercepting depots, but the land required for those depots was not included in that estimate, as there were see'eral lets yet under consideration. The committee therefore advised that the sum be £12,000. Councillor Suwon seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor Bunciess moved as as amendment that the re- commendation be not confirmed. He thought it was an ob- surd thing to put measles and whooping cough in the same category as scarlet fever, typhoid fever, and other infectious ' diseases. The argument seem:d to be that as there was only one patient in the hospital suffering from a disease, they should fill it with little children suffering from measles. It reminded him of bow Sir William Harcourt once said that they should alter the words of ths wise man venires vanitatum, omina vanitas " and say "sanites sanitatuat,omnia sanitas." If the sanitation proposed was the sort of thing they were going to have it seemed to him that the two phrases were almost synonymous. He thought the Council would not be willing to see the hospital made use of 'simply in order to meet cases of measles and whooping cough', which would always be prevalent. Councillor FLEMING seconded the amendment. Councillor FRANCOMB did not agree with the chairman of the Sanitary Committee. He foam] thtt there were only two members of the Sanitary Committee who had children under seven years of age, and the committee did not seem to have any feeling for those who had. (Laughter.) When arbitrary power was gained in 1879 it was, as was well known, pat into force in a most objectionable manner. (Hear, hear. and cries of " No." 1 They had had sights and scenes in the homes of the people of Warrington that hid been a disgrace to any body of men who sat on any Coun- cil. (Cries of "No,'' and a voice" Yes.") He had visited several houses, and never 8311, such abject poverty and men- tal suffering from people who were forced to pay large sums of money which they could not afford.—r The Mertes: Is it worth while to go into that matter ?]—He would like to say more. It seemed as though that arbitrary power was settling down into one law for the rich and another for the poor. The rich man kept his children at home and sent the other members of his family away, but that the poor man could not do, and his child must be dragged away by force. A mother was the proper nurse for a child, and not a hireling in a hospital. In his opinion,measlas and whoop- ing cough were spread principally by children attending school when suffering from them. Councillor MILNER thought the matter should be looked at with calmness. Infectious diseases should if possible be got rid of, and the only way to do so was to isolate cases. The work of the committee since they were granted compul- sory powers had beau highly satisfactory. The object of the Committee was not to fill the hospital, but to know exactly where cases of measles and whooping cough existed, so that measures could be taken to prevent a spread of the illness. The primary object of the resolution was to get compulsory notificitieo, and not removal. COURCIIIOI* ROBERTS said that the arguments that had been need to show that the Sanitary Committee had not ex- I ercisel their powers arbitrarily was a good reason fcat the extension of those powers. It might have been that at the outset the powers were somewhat strenuously exercised, but from a knowledge of facts be maintained that such was no longer the case. The large amount of eentiment with which Councillor Francemb had clothed his remark,a was entirely uncalled for. There was no difficulty in getting the chil- dren of the poor into the lvJspital. He also knew that in many cases the mothers to whom

.1 Councillor Prancomb had so chivalrously and men- ' timental:y referred were the worst nurses in such ; matters. In many cases the lives of children might have been lost had they not been rescued from their aurroua I- , ins. If notification was e.,mpulsory on the part of rro 'cal men, indiscriminate sending of children to school whilst suffering from these affections would no longer be possibl r. , He bad no hesitation in saying that the very valuable life a of Father Thomas would have been spared to Warrington r had notification been compulsory. He supported the com- mittee as one who had three children under seven Tears of age who bad suffered through the spread of measles. Councillor J. PrEuronsx did not think tbesuggestsd corn- ' pulsory power should he put in the hands of the commit. Itee. In some cases children would be better in hospital than at home, but taking it generally, and considering the large number and often trivial character of the cases, it I would be unwise to give the committee such arbitrary power. I He thought cases of measles and whooping cc u 411 were tri- via ones, not more than one or half per cent terminating fatally. He did not see how the case cf Father Thomas was applicable, as no application for his admissicn into tie hospital bad been made or refused.

Councillor MacittE supp;rte-d..--t.he resolution. If it had been suggested that compulsion in all cases was required he should not have agreed with it. He could not agree with the separation without consent of mother and child, but be ' did not understand that the committee had any wish to force that upon them. (A Voice : " Question.") Weil, it was a quest' m that the chairman or some responsible mem- ber of the committee could give them information upon. EAt this point interruptions by Councillor Whittle delayed the business a few moments until the Mayor advised the Councillor to read ltochefoucault's maxim that "the chief u'udy of man should be, to correct his own follies."] Con- tinning, Councillor Mackie said that they could not do better than throw open to the town that invaluable building —the hospital.

Councillor Soren?? thought it unfair to charge the com- mittee with want of feeling as the powers were only intended to refer to very poor people who were not able to give the required attention and suetenance to their children. The committee did not e ieb to force any one in the hos- pital who were capable of being taken care of at home, and the committee never endeavoured to force payment wt.ere the parties were too poor to pay. Councillor FRANCOMB maintained that the committee had tried to make poor people pay, but were stopped by the action of the council, since- when a better state of things had prevailed. Alderman CRI‘NDLEY asked if it was proposed that the measures should be compulsory or permissive. If it was permissive power, subject to the consent of the parties con- cerned, he should vote for the minutes. Alderman BURGESS said that it would be simply the no- tification that the disease existed in a house. (Cries of " No.") The medical officer bad no individual 'power of action and would simply have to report to the sanitary Committee. Alderman Burgesee having made use of the word " nonsense," in reference to remarks (hit had been made, Councillor BURGESS rose to a point of order an ailed if it was right to describe as "nonsense" the remarks of mem- bers of the Council. Alderman Burgess retaliated that if the Councillor felt aggrieved by the term, which, however, " was strictly correct as applied to him," he would with- draw it, and thereupon Councillor Burgess warmly insisted upon the Mayor ruling that the er.pression should be with- I drawn. The Mayor, however, did not think that "nonsense" Cams within the category of offensive expressions, and he naively remarked that an eminent writer said that nonsense was an essential ingredient in rendering sense acceptable to some minds. Councillor Burgess still demanded a 'with- drawal, and the Mayor made an appeal to his feeling by the remark that as the expression ca_ne from his uncle, Coun- cillor Burgess might excuse it. Apparently that gentle- man did rot sea the force of the argument, for he expressed himself afraid that he mast decline even to " make room for his uncle." (Laughter.) Algerman Burgess was detailing how the late Councillor Whittle used to dispose of differences of the present kind by nonchalantly declaring that it did not matter. as what had been said would be known whether it was withdrawn or not, when Committer Burgess objected to the matter being made light of in that manner. 'rhe Savoie repeated that the expression was not offensive, and Alderman BURGESS said he was surprised at the pertinacity of Committer Burgess, who then hotly demanded a with- drawal of that expression; he did not think it right that a member should be called pertinacious. The Alderman sar- castically told the Councillor to 'Go on." The latter then declared, emphasising it with a vimo-1-0139 blow on the table, that he would not "stand it," and immediately sat down.

The MAYOR, amidst laughter, remarked that the word "nonsense " was mild when compared to the term "jackal." Oat had been used in Parliament,. and the little scene then ended, and Councillor Burgess haying perhaps reflected on the dories of nephews, like " Tommy " in the song, " made room for his uncle."

Alderman &mows, continuing his original statement, said that if the parents of a patient were consenting parties the patient would be removed, If they were not the medical officer would ask the committee for authority to take the case to the magistrates, if thought expedient, and ask them for that power which would enable him to make the re- moval.

Alderman HOLMES said that it appeared to him after the explanations that had been given that all that was wanted was to obtain the medical officer's report to the Sanitary Committee on the existence el the cases. He thought it desirable that such exieteece should be known so that the necessary means could be employed. Councillor CROSFIELD, said that it was not proposed to give the Sanitary Committee any more power than they pos- sessed, and therefore he saw no sense in opposing it. The committee simply desired notiacatiou, and was it not infor- mation of which every member of the committee should be in possession P They as a commi:tee would hive no more compulsory power of removal than had been the case for the last three or four years. Councillor BROADBENT thouzht that the Council would take an unwise responsibility upon themselves if they re- jected the proposition. He was in favour of treating infan- tile diseases at home, anct it was only because he believed that the pawers about to be granted would be used with the greatest possible discretion by the committee that he should be willing to grant them. Alderman KEAN said he failed to see any attempt to gain arbitrary power, and should therefore support the recom- mendation-

In answer to Councillor Bolton, Alderman Brant:A gave his word that the same thing was done elsewhere, but did not enumerate any particular places. Councillor WHITTLN said he thought the committee wan- ted to fall the hospital to justify the expenditure upon it, and Couneillor Dolor,: expressed the con% iction that did the committee obtain compulsory powers they would lose no time in exercising them. Alderman Davtuaguoted from Act of Parliament to show that such power could not he given to the committee abso- lutely. The Act provided for removal after application to a ,ustioe in cases where necessary. Safety to the community was the sole and primary intention of the law; the health of the public was the primary, and that of the patient the secondary, consideration. Alderman BaltnEss, replying to the discussion, disclaimed any intention to interfere between parent and child, and said to should leave the matter to the good sense of the best informed members of the Council.

The amendment was then pat to the vote, with the follow- ing result :—For: Councillors J. Pierpoint, Burgess, Tingley, Fleming, Hutchinson, Francomb, Ashton, Marsh, Bolton, W. Pierpoint, Dixon, and Whittle (12) ; against: Aldermen Burgess, Kean, Holmes, Davies, and Chandley, Councillors Crostleld, Broadbent, Mackie, Milner, Wright, Dakin, Green- ing, Litton, Sutton, Roberts, and the Mayor (16). The amendment was therefore lost. The consideration of the other minntes.of the committee was proceeded with, and after some discussion, they were adopted with a few dissentients. The Council t'.eri ad- journed until Tupsday evening next, when the remainder of the business on the agenda will be taken.

On Thursday, William Rauscher and Ferdinand Kuelpin, charged with causing the death of A Jannsen, on the high seas, were brought up at the Bow-street Police Court, and remanded pending the arrival of formal papers from the Home Office. _ _

The prisoner Frederick Marshall was again brought up at'Woolwich, on Thursday, on the charge of murdering Laura Wilson. Further evidence was given as to the threats which the prisoner had used towards the girl, and his pos- session of a dagger which is now missing. A.nother remand was granted. Tee Marquis of Bute opened on Thursday the buildings of a new Roman Catholic Col'ege in Glasgow, intended to accommodate 300 students, and delivered an address in which he claimed for his Church the merit of being the pioneer in the work of higher education in Scotland as well as in that of national education. DEATH IN THE FOOTHILL FIELD.—A youth named Hugh Lewin, an apprentice bookbinder, died at Edinburgh from injuries received in the football field. He was playing in the Queen's Park on Saturday, when be received a violent kick in the stomach, whereby he was completely prostrated and made to suffer intense pain. A doctor attended him, but the unfortunate youth gradually sank. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 10, 1885.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN, in the excellent speech which he made at Birmingham, on Monday, referred to the future programme of the Lib- eral party, and in doing so he said :—" In the first place, I think, on the whole, the extension of popular authority will make for peace." It is significant thatthe rising hope of Radicalism in this country deals with the question of peace a a matter to be put "in the first place," and it is suggestive that he expresses a qualified opinion on the subject. The fact is the masses of our countrymen, if not carried away as Frenchmen are with the idea of glory, rather take to the metaphor of the British Lion. It is long since war with all its horrors was brought to our doors, and so long as there are hundreds of miles between us and actual slaughter, it would seem that we rather enjoy the prospect of the Lion pouncing on some weaker animal and crushing it with its ponderous jaws. There is a good deal of the brute in man as vet, des- pite all that centuries of training has' done for him; and what is wanted is to sub- judicate it more and more to the control of the mental and the moral faculties. It is not that we would have the English a nation of milksops; there need be no fear of that. But it would be a poor and miserable out- come of the extended suffrage if it resulted in John Bull becoming more bellicose. We hope for better things of democracy—that it will, as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has it, ".make for peace." But democracy requires to be enlightened, for we none of us sufficiently realize the terrible nature of war and the con- sequences of war. People are discussing this,' that, and the other cause of a world- wide depression in trade. The causes are numerous and varied, and war is not the least amongst them, , though it is too frequently I overlooked. We cannot spend twenty mil- lions on a war in Afghanistan without feel- ing it in other ways than its direct effect upon the exchequer. Dead men do not wear clothing; and killing our customers is therefore a poor way of encouraging trade. We get the chance, it may be, of providing them with shrouds, but shrouds,unlike shirts or headbands, do not want renewing. India was not at war with Afghanistan; but India suffered, and is suffering, in consequence, and, through India, Lancashire suffers to- day. The zso millions of people inhabiting our vast eastern Dependency are always liv- ing on the borderland of starvation. They spend little in food and less in clothing; and the climate being warm, they can do without clothing when they cannot do with- out food. It thus happens that when there is an extra pinch of poverty there is a falling off in the demand for cotton goods. That pinch came during the Afghan war ; th-t demand for our supplies raised the price of food ; and the exchequer was so low that the late Government were reduced to the miserable, the dishonourable expedient of appropriating moneys set aside as a Famine Fund. Need we be surprised, under such circumstances, that our trade with India is I

not what we would like it ? We are paying the penalty of past folly in the re3trlcted volume of trade, and India, poor India, is also called upon to pay the piper when she had no voice whatever as to the tune. Going back to the great civil w4r in the United States, we learn from " War and its conse- quences," by Professor LEVI —a little work published by Messrs. PARTRIDGE 45C Co. which should in the hands of every Re"

diture of 800,000 lives and ii,oomoo,ooo in money—a sum too vast to be realised. And how did this war—some two thousand miles from our shores, affect us ? Is it not written in history that by depriving us of cot- ton it produced a famine in Lancashire of the most heart-rending character? In 1860 our exports to the United States were over Ez r,000,000 ; in 1861 they fell down to less than fro,ooo,oco. But the rids- chief did not end there ; our American cousins, like the mother country, incurred a big war debt; but, unlike the mother country', they set about clearing it off as speedily as possible. To do this they had to resort to heavy taxation, and to heavy duties uP°l3 imported goods—thus doubly taxing the selves and injuring this and other countries by cutting off a certain amount of trade coo" nection. The Franco-German war of 187°- 7r, and the late war between Russia and Tur- key were similar to the war in America in being awfully destructive of life and propertY; Europe has to a large extent been drained oi both money and men during the last fifteen years, and the effect upon trade has unques- tionably been most disastrous. If TurlreY: egged on by Lord BEACONSFIELD, had 0' entered into war with Russia, we la,a,Y be quite sure that some of the roir lions of money that were expended 14 that worse than useless enterprise w°ll',, have found their way through trade channel: into this and other countries. As it is, b°t; Russia and Turkey have been impoverisheu ; and they are suffering with other nations fr°,,ttle the depression in trade. Something lits the same thing is going on at titi; moment in Egypt. Trade is dislocate 01 the forces of destruction instead of •those °t production have been at work, and tbaa. country, naturally rich and inhabited bYbe people more or less industrious, is on t, verge of bankruptcy. Already in this cowl there has been an addition to the income tali in consequence of war in Egypt; there Nod in all probability be another addition; 311,6 meantime Egypt cannot help, as she oil' could, to keep our looms and spindles rnillci fling. Democracy will not of course be Obeli upon directly to pay the war tax; but it Wlr nevertheless have to pay. It is the lot ooli the people to labour, and labour—whethe_r hand or brain—is the source of all wealth aPat of all payments to the State. This is Who those who are enfranchised, and those 11,0 are about to be enfranchised, require realise; and then there can be no quest.,,%l' that the extension of their autlaoritY "make for peace." Let them read histol and see how it comes about that we 11,3'4 to pay £27,000,000 annually in interest aJ°/ because our mad ancesters piled up a deb.: .£BOO 000,000 in prosecuting mad wars. .Ice them read such books as COBDEN'S " Tbir'n Panics" recently republished by the Cobu% Club, and they will then see how easy it is `I get up a mjlitary scare,_ and how costly it Tit% prove to the nation. Let them attend stiv, lectures as Mr. HOWES will give in Warri% ton this next week; and then they will how necess try it is for the people to trg ' their own affairs in their own hands. them put War and Education side by and see how much is spent on one and a e little on the other; let them judge each t NYr,eD by its fruits, and they will finally say ", LONGFELLOW : Were half the power that fills mankind with terr°„r: Were half the wealth bestowed on camps and cour"' Given to redeem the human mind from error, There were no need of arsenals nor forts. nre alike

being made to the magistrates, who, in turn, 'would have it in their power to grant an order for compulsory removal to the Hospital. It will thus be seen that the stringent power Which may finally be exercised is well safe- guarded; but the question is -whether it Ought to be exercised at all in cases of Ineasles.and whooping cough. For our part we think the Sanitary Committee have made Out a good case for giving the matter atrial, assuming that the cost will not be burdensome. Granted that these ailments come under .the head of minor diseases, it is surely sufficient tO "give us pause." when one of them alone has in half a year reduced the population by zoo souls: It may be that mothers would feel it when their little ones were taken from their arms; but better a short separation, With the hope of return, than the long sepa- ration when death ensue* throu?li nursing nder insanitary conditions—followed, it may °e, by the illness and death of others equally near and dear. If there were a doubt that the Chances of recovery would be lessened by re- to the Hospital, or if it were not Patent that isolation in the first instance is Athe best way of grappling with contagious rkiseasee, we should have more sympathy with "le stand taken by the opposition. THE SLEEPING-OUT NUISANCE AT WIDNES..—Mr. H. Gaskell, junr., at the Widnes Police Court, on Monday sentenced a boy named William Joseph Murray for sleep- ing in Messrs. Mitchinson's Chemical Works, and John McMahon for sleeping in the Alkali Company's Works, each to seven days hard labour. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—Yesterday, before Mr. John Brundrit, Thomas Sherlock was charged with making a false statement for the purpose of obtaining relief, and he was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.—John Wilson, alias W. Roach, and John Cross were convicted of begging, and were each sentenced to 14 days' bard labour. DRUNKENNESS AT WIDNES .At the Widnes Police Court on Monday the following persons were each fined for the offence of drunkenness :—Mary' Porter, Joseph Whiliambua, Michael Grahameand Anthony MeGloyne.—On Wednesday, for a similar offence, penalties were imposed upon Margaret Marshall, John Thos. Walsh, John Murray, Josiah Hough- ton, Joseph Santley, Peter Sparks, and James Lavin. RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly, meeting of this committee was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Briecoe was an the chair, and there were also present—Messrs J. Simpson, W. Handley, and J. D. Jones (ribrarian).—The Librarian's report for the past month was read.-1 he com- mittee adopted the list of books recommended by the Book Selection Committee to be purchased to the amount of £l6. They also recommended, the fixing of a newspaper reading stand in the reaeing-room.—Accounts amounting to £l6 5a 6d were passed for payment. A DITTON FARMER AND HIS TRACTION ENGINE. Thos. Wright, farmer, Dittos, was surnmoued before Messrs. Blinkhorn and Gaskell, junr., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charee of having, on the 24th of December, between sunset and sunrise, driven a traction en- gine along the highway at Ditton.—P.C. Hudson proved that on the day in question, sunset was at 3.52, and he met the defendant's engine at 5 20 —The defendant explained that he should have been home sooner, but he could not get a proper supply of water from the boiler. Under the cir- cumstances the Bench only imposed the light penalty of 2s. 6it and costs, 12s. 6d. A Gtormrsos TRAMP AT Renecoarr. -- Before Captain Hazlehurst at Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday, Michael Cadeyea tramp, was charged with making false statements for the purpose of obtaining relief.—P.S. Whalley stated that at ten o'clock on the previous night the prisoner asked for a ticket for a night's lodgings. He said he bad no money, but a search revealed the fact that he had Is 411 in his pockets. The prisoner explained that he had two pairs of trousers and he was not aware be had any money about him.—His worship said no man with commonsense and pro- fessing to be hard up, would expect such a statement to be believed, and he sentenced the prisoner to 14 days' hard labour. PIGEON SHOOTING MATCH FOR £so.—For the third time within the past three months Mr. James Welsby, of War- rington, champion shooter, journeyed to Oldham on Mon- day to contest a pigeon shooting match against Cocker Knott. of Oldham, the conditions being to shoot at 21 birds each, loz. shot, 21 yards rise, and 60 fall, to find birds and trap against each. other. The birds were of excellent quality, having been trained for the occasion, and one of those killed had been shot at in 14 matches. Over 600 persons were present, and betting was somewhat brisk at 21 to 20 on Weleby, who killed 13 out of 10, to Cocker Knott's nine out of 18, when the match ended in favour of the former. Mr. George Stead, of Ashton, was the referee. A STRUGGLE WITH A LUNATIC IN WID/09.—0n Mon- day, Mr. Seennell, relieving officer for Widnes, had a severe struggle with a lunatic, and but for the presence of mind which he displayed the probability is that bis life would have been sacrified. It appears that a labourer, named Bernard Crowley, who resided in lodgings in Cromwel' street, and who had been d. inking heavily since:, eeeteetmes. not into Buch an uncontrollable ceeitloll that he jumped e ben'ro iottl windost end dislocated one of his throughshoulders, hbesides otherWiee injuring himself. For seemral ' days he was strange in his demeanour, and at last his tone duct became of such a dangerous character that his landlady' applied for assistance and protection to the police,'and they referred her to the relieving officer. Early on Monday, Mr.' Scannell visited the house, and found Crowley in one of the bedrooms, with a large glass bottle in each hand, and also an iron missile. Crowley, laying down one of the bottlee, seized hold of the poker, and was about to use it, when Mr. Scannell overpowered him and took it from him. Dr. Cooper subsequently pronounced him to be insane. In the after- noon he was brought before Mr. F. H. Gossagr, J.P., at the Police Court, and that gentleman ordered his removal to Rainhill Aeylum, where he was afterwards taken by Mr. Scannell. CLAIM Fon ADVERTISING. At the Ste Helens County Court on Wednesday, before Mr. T. P. Thompson, judge, James Warwick, sewing maohine manufacturer, Manchester, was sued by Thomas Swales, of Widnes, for the recovery of £B, alleged to be due for advertising in the Widnes Weekly News, of which paper plaintiff is the proprietor. Mr. Peters, solicitor, Widnes, appeared for the plaintiff, and the defend- ant was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens.—Mr. Peters stated that the claim was for four quarter insertioas ,of an advertisement relating to the defendant's machines, ; and also for 230 copies of the Weekly News. The practical question between the parties was whether the order was for one insertion or for four quarters insertions, or whether or not it had at any time been countermanded. In September, 1883, the Farnworth Agricultural Society held theiv annual show at which Mr. Warwick (defendant) was an exhibitor. The plaintiff's reporter, Mr. Morewood, attended in his pro- fessional duty, and had an acquaintance with Mr. Warwick, to whim he spoke. Mr. Morewood subsequently stated the quarterly terms for advertising, and Mr. Warwicie thereupon told him to insert an advertisement all lib, and he would send on alterations in the advertisement which he might have to make. On the day following the issue of the paper in which the notice of de- fendant's machines appeared the defendant telegraphed for 200 copies of the paper, and they were suseplied.—Mr. Swift here interposed, and said his client had paid "53 into court for one insertion of the advertisement, and also paid for the papers supplied.—Mr. Peters stated that Mr. Morewood subsequently saw Warwick at Manchester, and the defend- ant promised "t,O send on the" change' advertisement. T lwr quarterly accounts for the advertisement were forwarded, and were not returned until the following July, when the defendant wrote stating that he had not authorised the ad- vertisement to be inserted more than once.--Evidence to this effect was given by the plaintiff, Thomas Swales (proprietor of the Wines Weekly News), and Mr. T. P. Morewood, re- porter.—Mr. James Warwick (defendant) deposed that nothing was ever mentioned about the terms for advertising, and that he only gave the order forttre advertisement to be Inserted in one issue of the paper. He had not the slightest idea that the advertisement was being inserted, and the first account he received he forwarded hack to the plaintffe with an intimation that he had not Indere its continuous inser- tion.—Mr. C. Howard, clerk and traveller in the emeloy of the defendant, proved that it was not a practice of the de- fendant to advertise in any paper a continuous modem of insertions—The Judge said there was so much coatradic- tem in the case that the only conclusion he could-corns to was that the plaintiff had not made out his claim satisfac- torily. He did not impute anything intentionally wrong, but is thought one might haveletgotten the circumstances and the other too anxious to tress his business, tHe would therefore enter a non-suit, with leave, with costs. An excellent programme of songs, Jrc., was gone through, and the meeting concluded with the usual votes of thanks. A DISHONEST BOATMAN AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, Henry Knipe, a young man, employed as a boatman at Manchester, was charged with stealing from a stable at Preston Brook, a horse strap, value 2s, the property of Fellows, Morton, Jr. Co., carriers, Wolver- bampten. It appeared that Alfred Bourne, boatman for the prosecutors, put his horse up in a stable at Preston Brook, on the night of the 16th December. Next morning he discovered that a strap had been taken from his horse. George Ricketts, a boatman, also experienced a similar loss. Subseqneutly the straps were recovered at Barnton, where the prisoner had disposed of them. The prisoner WAS Ap- prehended at Manchester and given into the custody of P.C. Wynne. The magistrates (Messrs J. Brundrit and James Reynolds), sentenced the prisoner to 14 days', hard labour.

FATALITY AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS. INQUEST ESTERDAY. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Widnes Accident Hospital, yesterday, touching the death of Michael Lennon, a labourer, who died in that In- stitution on Monday last. Mr. A. S. Richmond, H.M. in- spector of factories, was present. Mr. C. H. Lewin appeared to watch the proceedings on behalf of Messrs. James Mils- pratt and Son, and there were also present Mr. Lewis, manager to the firm, and Dr. Eschellmann.— Miss Downie, matron of the hospital, having given evidence. Thomas Burnes, of Railway-street, said the deceased was 27 years of age, and lived at a lodging-house in Lugsdale-read. Wit- ness and the deceased were employed under Mr. Drury, but on the let instant they were engaged removing barrels, which would weigh about 4cwt. from a new shed to a weighing machine by order of Tim Braman. The last barrel was within four inches of a well which was about three feet from the surface of the ground to the surface of the liquor. The deceased went round the barrel to push it away, and walked into the well. He commenced screaming, and wit- ness shouted for help and waited WV Joim ':4113e up. They then pulled deceased out of the well. Without as- sistance the deceased ran to a cold water tap, removed his elythes, and allowed the water to run upon his body. De- ceased was subsequently taken into the watchman's hut and oil applied to his injuries, and was afterwards conveyed to the accident hospital in a cab. Mr. F. Jolley said that at the time of the accident the well contained 16 inchta of chloride magnesia, which did not burn at all unless hot. The liquor was wann. At the tims of the accident. Mr. Lewfs, manager at the works, described a plan of the qusi ta shed where the accident.oCCatreds id an experimental process was carried on thsfe.;—Affer the Coroner tau illumined up, the jury returned a verdict that the deceased died from the effects of scalds received whilst in a delicate state of health. Mr. Lewin observed that Messrs. Muspratt, although the deceased was not in their employ, intended to bury him decently.

The nest business was the report of the Parliamentary Boundary Committee, and at the request of the Chairman Mr. Lightburn made a statement. He said at a special meeting held on the 18th December, a deputa- tion consisting of Messrs Lake, Fisher, Nor- man, Speakman, Lightburn, and the chairman, was appointed to take steps for having Runcorn made the centre of one of the Parliamentary divisions of Cheshire. The object of the deputation was to ha strictly confined to giving the name of Runcorn to the district with which the town was associated, and he might say that Mr. Shaw, the chairman, kept entirely to the duty the deputation had been sent to perform. (Hear, hear.) lint strange to say, at the meeting before the Government Commissioners, one of the gentlemen—it was Mr. Norman—stated that the Board of Commissioners believed that the boundaries as set forth by the Government Commissioners was the best one. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Lightburn) was struck with as- tonishment. The deputation cat rather a tr. rry figure, for there were three members contradicting one another.
