Sir,—ln answer to a letter signed" Tee Tee" in your last bane, please allow me space for a brief reply. He says my reasoning is not at all clear, thoueh he seems to have thoroughly understood me and endeavoured to make a little capital oat of the part I omitted about Christ being celled a glutton. He then tries to throw doubt on the whole by asking if we believe j)lat John the Biptist was possessed of a devil. "Tee Tee' wants to. know where the sting would be if Christ had been an abstainer, I answer him nowhere, just as there would have been no sting in the remark that he was a gluttonous man if He bad been a great abstainer from foot. John came practising great abstemiousness in food and dress; his life to the people appeared a most mel- ancholy oneeand they said he was possessedby an evil spirit. Our Saviour ate and drank much the same as themselves (that is the temperate ones) and they said he was a glut- tonous man, and a winebibber. Ili each case they had a certain amount of troth to base their false charges on. And now I wish to ask "Tee Tee" his opinion of the wine our Saviour speaks about when he says men put new wine in new wine bags." Was it not that the pure jaice of the grape fermenting (in obedience to a natural iaw) would have more space by the new skins stretching? "Tee Tee" wants some facts to enlighten him as to the condition of the Jews, and of Christ condemning their drunkenness. If he will read vol. 4of Dr. Geikie's " hours with the Bible he will foil that in Old Testament times they were much worse than I described them, and Jam not aware he can point out any improvement in after years. If, too, he will consult an article in the " iVit'sh and Foreign Evangelical Review" by Dr. Blaikie, be will be enlightened as to how it was that our Saviour did not attack the social evils of His time. Again, if he will look through the late Dean Stanley' "History of the Jewish Church," he will find I was not far wrong in stating that there were Teetotal Societies in the time of Chr;st. I hope" Tee Tee will not consider these "Indifferent witness'; also that after due consideration, he will give us his "inferences." I quite agree with him in hie concluding remark as to the evils of drunkenness ' • also when he says that the New Testament is the great battle. ground of moderatwe, as there our position is impregnable, and ab.stainers w isting their time . and energies in try- ing to obtain a footing. They should consider it no battle- ground for them.—Yours very reepectfully, . MODERATOR.

Sir,—Your contemporary bee a letter signed " A Dis- gusted Moderator," in which all teetotallers are character- ised as a sect of bigots and as wanting in reverence for Christ, and respect for one of England's greatest statesmen, Mr. W. E. Gladstone. They are also charged with branding the thoughtful and respectable moderator with the stigma of drunkenness. I have been, Sir, a teetotaller for 30 years, and I have had a great deal to do with the formation of total abstioeuce societies, and as a censequeuce I have taken part in the meeting', and on behslf of myself and a large number of my teetotal friends, I most emphatically deny the charges brought against us; and if that enlight- ened moderator would cast the beam out of his own eye he would SO3 clearly how to cast th 3 mote out of the eye of a teetotaller. And now, Sir, I will answer the first question asked by Moderator, which is was Christ a teetotaller, by asking another—Wai\ Christ a Nezarite ? and, if so, is it not said "He shall not drink wine nor strong drink?" Did He come to break the law? Certainly not; and for a minister of the Gospel to say Christ was not a teetotaller was, to say the least of it, an unwise thing. We are told, says "Moderator," that Christ turned water into wine and that He was accused by the Pharisees of being a wine bibber. Bat for "Moterator," or anyone else, to say that the water became alcoholic wine, is an assumption made and then put forward as an objection. It was wine they say, and that is enough ; but what Christian could believe that when men were drunk Christ provided a further supply of the Intoxicant? What! 120 gallons of intoxicating liquor pro. vided by Christ for men to drink when men were drunk. As Dr. Lees says in his Temperance Bible, this assumption is wholly without proof, and it involves a reflection upon the wisdom of the Son of God which ought to insure its rejec- tion by every reverential mind. "Moderator "says something about Christ being called a wine bibber ; but that does not prove that he was on the side of those who pride themselves with the saying—" let your moderatien be known untn all men." Query: Is it modera- tion to use poison as an ingredient of our foods? What is moderation? Moderation is living by measure. Now what is the true measure of the life of a Christian? Is it not to found in the .cross of Christ ? Which then is the more moderate man, tbat is which regulates his life more ac- curately according to the measure of that cross, the man who to the peril of the weak parades his liberty to drink, or he who abstains for the sake of others? When the mea- sures of men's lives are drawn from eternity, ills a ques- tion worthy of consideration, whether the teetotaller is not accerding to these measures the true moderate man. But " Disgueted Moderator," should know there is no such psseage as the one to which we have referred. The revised yereion reads "Let your forbearance be known to all men," or "let your gentleness be known unto all men." Surely the man who is a teetotaller for exemple's sake has a right to claim that in this reenact, at all events, he is let- ting his gentleness be known unto all men. He does not aa- sort his rights to the injury of the weak. I hope that" A Disgusted Moderator" before he rashes into print agaia will got his bible, and, instead of trying to put down what the Church of Christ bas of late been doing for the destruction of one ef the most appalling and dire evils, he will read the warnings found therein against the subtle seductiveness of intoxicating drink and the danger connected with the use of it even in small quantities. The histories of Noah and Lot show us how dangerous it is even for good men to use intoxicants, and how easily they may be betrayed into over-indulgence. These two narratives are a standing warning t ) those who think they stand, to "take heed lest they fall ;"and allow ma to say in conclusion that if what has been done in more thenone Wesleyan chapel on:Temperance Sunday is to be the outcome of it, the sooner , the Wes:evan Conference give it up the better. If what l the preacher referred to about Christ not being a teetotaller be true, why then no teetotaller can get to heaven, for he can never be like Christ. But, happily for us teetotallers, i we have learned better things, and if any hearer in a Wes- leyan chapel should fall through what was said respecting Christ, on whom will the responsibility rest ? Will either ' the minister or the " Disgusted Moderator" have the con- soling thought—" lat least delivered my soul ; I did for I him or her what I could." No, certainly not. Now, sir, I. ' think it would do the rev, gentleman more honour to con- fess his error, or at least withdraw the observation, which, to my mind, was uncalled for. The impression left on the minds of many is that it was done out. of an antagonistic spirit, and some have come to the conclusion never to bear him preach again. In the Irish Christian Advocate, a writer commenting on Mr. Wesley's views on the drink traffic, i says it modern teetotallers were to use such language, hard things would be said of them. Yes, perhaps, harder things than even "A. Disgusted Moderator" says about U 3. On this question our venerable founder knew how to call a spade a spade. I would that all who name his name would observe the same rule.—Yours, ,
A TOTAL ABSTAINER.

RAFFLES AT BAZAARS. Sir,—Your correspondent " Fair to All " has chosen a very misappropriate NOM de. plume. Such a one as " More than fair to some and less than fair to others" would have more suitably closed his epistle. He admits that lotteries are illegal, but he seems to claim exemption from the opera- tion of the law for some, while quite willing to hand others over to the tender mercies of Puritanical magistrates. On what ground he makes this claim is not very clear— whether on the ground of the unfairness of the law, or on that of the motives of the law breakers. If he contends that the law which makes lotteries illegal is not a good or well- considered law, there are plenty who think that people can- not be made virtuous by Act of Parliament, and that laws ought not to be made to save fools from their folly, who will agree with him. But that a law is not good is no reason why it should be made worse by not being applied impartially. He asks you to define the distinction between a draw tor a Liverpool lottery ticket and a draw for a Bel- gian lottery ticket. The simple answer is that there is no distinction t ) draw. Then he asks, "If the law of England would commit the speculator in an English lottery ticket to the degrade' ion of imprisonment, why should the same law permit thousands of foreign lottery tickets to be circulated through this country continually?" The answer to this is that the law of England does this for the same reason that it punishes a delinquent bank manager or forger who is in England, while It does not punish the delin- quent bank manager or forger who is in Spain, or any where else beyond the jurisdiction of extra- dition treaties, that is to say, because the foreign circulators of tickets cannot be got at. If I am not mistaken, when the Birmingham authorities first began to move in this matter it was saggested that the issuers of these foreign tickets should be punished, but the difficulties in the way of getting at them were so great that the idea had to be given up. Then as to the motives, your correspondent says the bare ides of his being called a rogue and vagabond be- cave he went to a Wesleyan baztar, got up for the purpose o! raising money for new schools, and there patronised the lucky bag, makes him laugh. Now, I should like to know If your correspondent is not compounded of the same flesh and blood as other men are. If he is, it is, legally, just as easy to set him down a rogue and vagabond as anybody else. He might laugh, hut be would in the eye of the law be a rogue and vagabond all the same. Then, again, one feels curious to know how far he is will- ing to allow his doctrine of motives to carry him. He might have varied his illustration and said Do you mean to say that, if I put my hand into somebody else's pocket and took out five shillings and handed them over to help to erect Wesleyan schools, you would call me a pickpocket r I leave tho Mayor in his judicial capacity to answer this query. Let us consider the application of this doctrine of motives a little farther. At the moment I write there stande condemned to death a German Socialist. Reinsdorf, for having attempted to take away the lives of his Emperor and other high dignitaries. There was nothing mercenary or ignoble about this man's motives. His object was to re- deem the masses of his fellow-countrymeu from their misery and social degradation. Yet will your correspondent main- tain that in this instance because of the motive the clime ought to be condoned? The truth is that no motive which prompts people to break the law can safely be recognised as a justification of the offence, and If the chief magistrate of a town says that it can, then all I will say Is that we ought to be well pleased that each court in which justices' justice Is administered is provided with a competent legal adviser. But I cannot help thinking your correspondent has taken the Mayor rather too seriously on this point, and 1 fancy

Without leaders and without funds it I would be Impossible to form an industrial party for the purpose of supporting an independent candidate, but the next best thing would be to form such a party as by united action we might almost dictate the terms on which any t candidate should be elected. There must be unity of action. We must forget that there such places as Soudan, Foochoo, Tonquia, and Timbuctoo. "A spirited foreign policy " that snare of English political life—must be replaced by a spirited domestic policy. Even the Disestablishment herring must not be allowed to take us off the scent,., and other projectedreforms must be left in abeyance until our rights are respected and our claims met. We have been too long betwixt the hammer of political injustice and the anvil of hard necessity. We intend to submit no longer. We have the vote now, and its value kas at last begun to dawn upon our dim intellect. We shall now want sorrothing more than a pint of beer for our vote. The,- rich have controlled legislation in their own interests- long enough; we claim our share of raat power. We are bound to obey the laws, and we intend to have a hand in making them, and then. it will be easier for us to keep them. I may be charged with advocating class legislation. What else have we ever had 2 I propose to add another class to the legislators. There will then be three, the Upper, Middle, and Lower, with a fair field and no favour, and I think the lower class will be able to give a good account of itself. Hitherto the class to which I belong has taken little or no interest in politics, believing, and doubt- less truly, that "one party was like the other, only worse." As this class has not come within the contaminating circle of party political wire-pullinz, there is a possibility of their forming a pare party which shall seek by just legislation to ameliorate the admittedly hard lot of their fellows, produc- ing contentment among the people, which will be the best zuarantee for the stability of the empire.—Yours, drc., Runcorn, January sth, 1835. WARRINGTON' BOARD OF GUARDIANS: The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. There were present Messrs Greening (chairman), Broadbent, Blackhurst, Jolley, Derbyshire. Appleton, 13,0wn, Owen, John Houghton. Wm. Houghton, Gibson, Greenell, Humphreys; Grange, Rev. G. F. Roberti, Cooper, Bonnet! ; J. C. Sutton (clerk)and S. Sutton (assistant clerk). ALTERA:MiI AT THE vronattomm. ' The House Comrnitt4 recommended with regard to the application for the enlargement of rooms by the workhouse master and mistress, that the proposed alterations be carried oat.—Mr. BROWN moved, and Mr. JOLLEY seconded the adoption of the minntes.—Mr. B LACEHURST thought that when an important minute like that we, recommended they ought to have someinfoi mation as to why it was recommen- ded. For his part she did not see why they should throw a , great deal of money away, as it would cost something like £BO or £lOO. He did not see why the ratepayers' money should be thrown away on what was only a fad; and I he moved ,as an amendment that the matter be referred ' back.—Mr. Aroma-rots said that the room as it was was too small, and be did not think the application was an unreason- able one. He supported the proposal of the committee.— Mr. Joust lionanrox said the room had done a long time and it might do a little longer.—Mr. JOLLEY defended the proposal of the committee, and eald the alterations would not cost either LSO or £loo.—Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON asked how many rooms the master had for his private use. —The CLERK sail there was one for the master and one for the matron.—Mr. BROADBENT supperted the proposal of the I committee, as he thought they would it make the proposal without having properly considered the matter.—Mr. JEANS thought the matter was one of those which might be post- poned as the rates were very high at present—Mr. OWEN said that at the present time farmers had to put off any im- provements which they had to make, and he thought this one might at present be postponed—After some further discussion the amendment was put and voted for by eight Guardians, the same number voting against ; the amend- "oent was consequently not carried. On the motion that the minute WA the voting was the some, and the chairman gave his casting vote to favour 9i the committee's proposal, Mr. Jeans did not vote. SCHOOLS CON WITTEE. The Schools Committee recommended that Mr. Mines, the master, be instructed to go to Swinton schools to gather Information there as to the management of the school.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said be could see that in the distance a great expenditure would be necessary to put the school yards in a proper con- dition. The yard was at present in a very bad condition, owing no doubt to the frost and thaw. With regard to warmer clothing for the children, a matter which had been called attention to by Mr. Broadbent, the doctor recom- mended that the extra clothing be got. He thought that the improvements to the yard would cost something like £2OO. and the clothing would also be an extra expense.—Mr BLACKHURST seconded the adoption of the committee's pro- posal, and suggested that the chairman of the committee accompany Mr. Mines.—Mr. BROADB NT, Mr. APPLETON, and. Mr. JEANS supported the proposal of the committee, the two latter suggesting that if it was necessary that the chil- dren should have extra clothing, it should be got at ence,— The minutes of the committee were adopted.
THE FESTIVITIES.

A KIND OFFER. The CHAIRMAN said be had just had put in his band a letter from Mr. W. Harmston, offering, if it was agreeable to the Guardians, to allow the children at the Workhouse to see the performance at the circus free of charge on Saturday, or should the weather prove unfavourable on that day he should be happy to admit them on the Saturday afterwards.—Mr. BLACKHURST asked if that invitation would include the children at Padgate.—The CHAIRMAN said that it would.—Mr. BLecsnurtsr said it was a very kind offer on the part of Mr. Harmston, and he should move that it be acceoted —The CHAIRMAN seconded this proposal, which was carried, several Guardians expressing the opinion that it was a very kind offer. NEWTON VACANCY —The CLERK intimated that he had received the order te fill up this vacancy on the Board. This concluded the businesq.

A Snocamo DEATH occurred at a public-house in Wol- verhampton on Wednesday morning. A brewer, named George Jones, was sitting on the edge of a copper of boil- ing wort, when he overbslanced himself and fell in. The poor fellow was got out as quickly as possible, and was taken to the hospital, where, after excruciating agony, death put an end to his sufferings.

MURDER AND StumnE.—A horrible discovery was made at Laughton, a village about six miles from Lewes, on Thursday morning. Two brothers, named John and Amos Barber, aged 55 and 65 respectively, occupied a little cot- tage at Laughton Pound, and earned kliving by shoemak- ing. In consequence of a letter which their yotrager brother sent to a man named Burton, who resides in the locality, saying he intended to commit suicide, Police-constable Gillham went to the Barbers' house on Thursday morning at nine o'clock. Being unable to make anyone hear, be broke the back door open, when he found the house empty. On going to a wood shed at the back of the premises he saw the eldest brother lying on the ground with his head bat- tered, and the younger hanglng by a rope to a beam above. Both were quite deid. SERIOUS FIRE AT CHESTER: EXCITING SCENE.—EarIy on Wednesday morning an alarm was given that a fire had broken out five doors from "God's Providence House," the historic old building in Watergate-street-row, Chester. The confligation was raging on the ground-floor premises of a trunkmaker named Hillhouse. The fire quickly seized the staircase' and shut off all means of escape inside for Mr. and Mrs. Hillhouse and the three children, who occupied the upper rooms. Presently Mr. Hillhouse appeared at the window amid the blinding smoke, and said that if they were not speedily rescued they must succumb to the flames. I . Happily the fire escape was quickly available, and the un- conscious forms of Mrs. Hillhouse and the three children were passed through to one of the firemen,and then Mr. Hill- house escaped in the Came way. Artificial respiration had to be resorted to in order to restore the children, who were unconscious for some time. The house and contents are gutted. No explanation is offered of the origin of the fire. REnisritimrriox.—ln a letter to a North-east Lancashire inquirer, Mr. Howel Thomas writes, on behalf of the Boun- dary Commissioners, that the whole scheme of redistribu- tion embodied in the Seats Bill is based upon population. No account whatever is taken of freehold voters for counties whose qualifications exist in either boroughs or comity divisions. If, however, the number of such voters is con- siderable, the Commissioners have a discretion allowed to them of assigning a smaller population to the electoral area in wkich the freeholders would vote. It is stated that the Coneervatives of North-east Lancashire will propose a division of that constituency into the four electoral areas of Accrington, Darwen, Clitheroe, and Rossendale. The Town Clerks of Leeds and Bradford have received communications from the Assistant Boundary Commissioner respecting the I boundaries of the five end three divisions into which these boroughs hive been respectively cut up. In both cases the plans differ from those submitted by the two political parties. It will be observed that the new constituencies are to be named after the geographical divisions of the boroughs.

EXPENDITURE OF NEW lON COMMISSIONERS. The Finance Committee of the Newton Improvement Commis- sioners, at a meeting on the 15th ult., passed accounts amounting to £359 83 ld. THE DITERSION OF SEWAGE FROM THE SWEET CANAL. —With reference to the notice of the London and North- Western Railway Company to local authorities that within the next six months all sewage running into. the Sankey Canal must be diverted, the Highway and Sanitary Com- mittee of the Newton Improvement Commissioners have ordered the surveyor to reply that the Commissioners have given instructions for the surveyor to complete his plans for the diversion of the sewage from the canal at the Earles- town (west) outlet as soon as circumstances will admit of its being done. THE RECENT EPIDEMIC OF SCARLET FETER.—The announcement that the Earlestown and Newton district is at present comparatively free from scarlet fever will give great satisfaction throughout the neighbourhood. The authorities appear to have thoroughly mastered the epidemic, I and though a few old cases are still lingering on towards re- covery, not a single new outbreak has been reported during the past fortnight, and there have been no deaths. It is stated, however, that a large number of children have been afflicted with measles, though not of a very dangerous or virulent form.

TISE BURNING FATALITY AT Sr. HELENS' JUNCTION.— An inquest was held on Monday afternoon at the Alexandra Hotel, Sutton, near St. Helens on the body of Mary Jane Fowles, thirteen months old, Who was fatally burnt on New Year's Day. Mrs. Fowles was proceediag upstairs at one a me with a paraffin lamp in one hand and her little daughter in the other arm, and when at the top of the stairs she stumbled and fell backwards to the bottom. The lamp was broken, and their clothes set on fame Both were severely burned, the result being that the child died a few kours afterwards, and Mrs. Fowles is still confined to bed, suffer- ing from burns, bruises, and shock to the system. A ver- dict of " Accidental death" was returned. THE NEW CEMETERY: IMPORTANT ARRANGEMENTS,— The work in connection with the new cemetery for Earles- etown and Newton will, it is expected, be completed in the course of the next few weeks, and the final arrangements for its opening for interments are being made by the Newton Improvement Commissioners. It is stated that tbe com- mittee have decided that the portion of land lying west of the main drive and the chapel shall be allotted for the in- terment of persons who have been connected with the ' Church of England; the land lying between the north boundary and the chapel, and east of the main drive will be used for Nonconformists; and the plot of land south-east of the chapel will be reserved as the Roman Catholic por- tion. The grave spaces to be held in perpetuity will be divided into three classes, A, 11, and C, in each denomina- tion, and the fees will be £5, £3, and £1 respectively for each single breadth. The same fees at present paid to (ha minister and sexton at Wargrave church will be adopted for the Church of England portion of the cemetery. Other charges which the committee decided upon have been sub- mitted to each member of the Board of Commissionerm, who will have to confirm or otherwise reject these arrange- ments.

NEWTON FOOTBALL CLIIB ANNUAL BALL.—The fourth annual ball in connection with the Newton Football Club was held in the Assembly-room of the Newton Town Hall on Friday evening. In preparation for the occasion the room had been tastefully decorated with bunting, lace cur- tains, Bre, and along the walls were suitable mottoes, a prominent one being " Success to our Patrons." The deco- rations had been effectively carried out by Messrs G. Lane, Braddock, Boardman, Mee, McCormick, Fairclough, Willis, and other members of the club. Dancing commenced ehortly after tine o'clock, and Stirrup's string band, which had been engaged for the occasion, rendered the music in a satisfactory manner. About 65 couples attended, and every- one apparently enjoyed themselves to their heart's contenot. The duties of Masters of Ceremonies were efficiently carried out by Messrs T. Fairclough and F. Willis, and the prom gramme had been gone through about five o'clock on the following morning, when the party broke up. It may be stated that the club is at present in a very prosperous con- dition. Up to the new year the first team had played seven matches, winning four and losing three ; and the second team had not been beaten in either of the six matches they had played. NEwros-LE-WILLows DOGS AT FOUR OAKS FAME.— Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton, nominated several of his dogs to compete at the Four Oaks Park meeting, which commenced on Tuesday. The principal event on the card was the Royal Manor Stakes, for 34 all-aged dogs at 1.03 each, with £5O added, and Mr. Stone's dogs Seaport and Satirist ran. In the first ties the first-nanted was de- feated by Mr. Burgess's Ballymonv, while Satirist, a clever deg, WAS thrown out by Mr. Jones's Hopeful Sammy. Satirist was one of the warmest favourites, and his defeat caused a sparring correspondent to write—" Satirist did not behave very well in his course with Hopeful Sammy, and gave his backers cause to regret that they bld laid such odds as two and three to one on him." In the Sutton Stakes, for 16 puppies at £3 10s each, Mr. Stone's Sarcastic beat Mr. Cochrane's Captain 111. in the first ties, and on the following day (Wednesday) splendidly disposed of Mr. Wilke's Wild Blackfellow. In the Streatley Stakes, for 10 all-aged dogs at £3 10s, Mr. Stone's Skipping Rope easily threw Mr. Darlington's Douceur out c. 4 the first ties; and in the second round capitally defeat2d Mr. Dale's Dustman. On Thursday Sarcastic was beaten by Mr. Wall's Waitress in the Sutton Stakes ; but in the Streetley Stakes Skipping Rope threw out Mr. Braithwaite's Winifred. The stakes were subsequently divided by Mr. Stone and Mr. Abbott, the latter's dog Gay Girl and Skipping Rope being the last two in thi course,

THOILtS Einzer.—The report that Mr. Thomas Hint, of Crow-lane.had been seized with a . sudden and dangerous illness while attending service inlVar- grave church OD Sunday forenoon last, created a general feeling of sympathy for that gentleman. Mr. Hunt is an old resident in the neighbourhood, and for some years has actively interested himself in matters affecting the toweshio and other local interests; and occupies thepositions of one of the Guardians of the Warrington union and one of the Im- provement Commissioners for the Newton township. As usual, be attended the service at Wargrave chur3h en Sunday fore- noon' and while sitting in his pew he became suddenly ill. •Some alarm was occasioned, and this was increased when Mr. Hunt had to be removed to.the vestry, where he was attended by Dr. Handyside, of Earlestown, and Mr. A. Peake, chemist and druggist, of Earleetown (both of whom, fortunately, were present in church). Mr. Hunt rapidly grew worse, and he was thereupon conveyed to the residence of the Rev. Canon Whitley, the sector. On the following day Mr. Hunt was removed to his home, and as he was hi a most dangerous state in the afternoon Dr. White, of War- rington, was called in. Mr. Hunt has since been under the medical treatment of Drs. Handyside and White, and it is a pleasure to record that on Thursday Mr. Hunt was a little better. For a considerable time past Mr. Hunt has been a sufferer from heart disease, and it was a serious attack of that complaint which seized him on Sunday forenoon. CHRISTMAS TREE AT NEWTON.. On Saturday evening the annual Christmas tree and distribution of prizes in con- nection with the Sanday schools attached to St. Peter's Church, Newton, took place in the schoolroom. The decoration of the tree lathe sole work of the Misses McCor- yodels, and was laden with all kinds of useful and fancy artistes in endless variety' and formed an irresis- table ahraction to the large number of juveniles who attended. Its illumination by several lanterns considerably enhanced its pleasing appearance. Dur- ing the evening the fair donors distributed to the scholars the articles with which the tree was laden, for which the hearty thanks of the recipients were expressed. The teachers and scholars in the Sunday school also received,prizes for their good attendance during the past year, the awards being formally handed out by Mrs. George McCorquodale. A series of dissolving views illus- trating scripture scenes, were subsequently exhibited by Mr. A. L. Evans, of Haydock, and several local illustrations, in. chiding Newton Church, and portraits of Colonel George McCorquodale and the Rev. H. Monk (vicar of the pariah) were warmly received.. The proceedings were interspersed with singing by the scholars, who had refreshments given to them during the evening. A very pleasant evening was spent, and the party separated about ten o'clock. Among the persona who attended during the evening were Colonel George McCorquodale, Mrs. McCorquodale, Miss Ilkley, Mr. A. C. McCorquodale; Mr. N. McCorquodale, Mr. Rirley, Mrs, Frank Raley, Miss McCorquodale, Rev. H. Monk, dm.
DINNER OF MESSRS. McCORQUODALE AND CO.'S
EMPLOYEES AT NEWTON.

One of those pleasant social gatherings which tend so much to foster and maintain that kindly feeling which. ought to exist between the employer and the employed took place at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton-le-Willows, on Satur- day evening. The occasion was the first annual dinner eif the compositors, pressmen, and machinemen engaged at the extensive printieg works of Messrs. McCorquodale and Co., Limited, at Newton-le-Willows, one of the largest establishments of the kind, if not the largest, in the kingdom. Mr. A. McCorquodale and Mr. Joseph F. Woods, the new manager, who is aleo one of the principal members of this enterprising and prosperous firm, haying not only expressed their approval of the gathering, but contributed liberally towards the feast. The dinner provided by Mr. and Mrs. H. Bond was a capi- tal one in every respect, while the waiting arrangements, an element of considerahle importance at meetings of this kind, leit nothing to be desired. In addition to the local employee a few old friende, "comp u formerly employed at the Newton Works, but now engaged in Manchester, Liverpool, and elsewhere, were present, and contributed to thO harmony O4lç eVening. Mr. Robert Eiindley, one of the principal overseers ir foremen in the compositors' room, occupied the chair, supported on the right and left by Mr. H. A. Glover (reader), Mr. John Hunt, and ether members of the committee, The printed programme, which embrace& in addition to the toasts customary on such occasions, piano- ' forte solos by Mr. J. Leyland and Mr. Helliwell, the latter officiating as accompanist to the vocal music ; songs, respectively by Messrs It Beere, J. Hunt, Philip Deakin, D. ' Bartlett, Frederick Appleton, Lennox, G. Wood, P. Perci- val, S. Clough, Duncan Cameron, and others ; and humor- ous recitations by Mr. J. B. Langan, was admirably carried Out with but little deviation the efforts of each performer being deservedly appreciated by the assemblage generally. On the tables being cleared and grace haying been said, the usual loyal toasts were given from the chair and right ley- ' ally reseonded to, followed by "The army, navy, and vol- unteers." proposed by Mr. J. Williamson. The Vice-Chair- man, in a conciee and exceedingly appropriate speech, in which he referred to the great improvements made in con- nection with the art of printing during recent years, and the inestimable blessings which the press conferred upon the nations at large, gave "The Prese," to which the Chairman responded, Mr. Langan on being called upon, replying to that part of the toast relating especially to the newspaper press.—In proposing the toast of the eyeving—" Health and prosperity to Messrs McCorquodale and Co., Limited,"— the Chairman aptly referred to the gratifying fact that there were so many old servants, both in the composing rooms and the machine department. With the exception of about eve years, he himself had been cennected with the eetab- lishment from the year 1851 no to the present time, while others belonging to some of them were growing up, as it were, at the works, a proof in itself that the firm was a good one. (Applause.) He trusted that the establishment in which those assembled were employed might long continue to prosper, and that they might all live long to enjoy the annual social reunions which they were now inaugurating. —The toast was received with hearty cheering and rnusical honours.—A similar compliment, proposed by Mr. Board- man, was paid to the foremen of the composing and machine departments, and it was briefly but felicitously ac- knowledged by the Chairman on behalf of himself and Messrs. John Dick and Galloway.—The Secretary Mr. H. A. Glover laid before the company a report of the proceedings connected with the getting up of the present inaugural dinner. He remarked that the object of their annual dinner was to encourage a more friendly and sociable feeling between their fellow-workmen, their fore- men, and their employers. (Applause.) Judging from the present gathering he had no hesitation in saying that the promoters of the festivity had in a great measure gained their point —Other toast., including "The Chairman and Vice-chairman " and " The host and hostess," .were also cordially drank, the company, which sat down to dinner at 5-30, separating in the best of humour shortly after 10-30 p.m.

STEALING SKATES AT PRESCOT.—A lad naraed George Allman was charged at the Preseot Petty Sessions, on Tues- day, with stealing a pair of skttes' value 4s 6d, from the shop door of Mr. Morton, pawnbroker, Eccleston-street, on the 29th ult. The lad was seen to take the skates from the shop door, and be was afterwards apprehended. He pleaded guilty, and the Bench imposed a fine of five shillings' and ordered the prisoner to receive twelve strokes with a birch rod.

ABIISING A FRIENDLY SOCIEYY CoLLECTOA.—Before Messrs A R Gladstone and F W Earle, at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday Mary Melia, a married woman residing in Kernble-street, was summoned for using defamatory lan- guage to Thomas Belton Melia on the 23rd December,—Mr T Swift, barrister, appeared for the complainant.—The com- plainant is an agent and collector in the employ of the Liverpool Victoria Friendly Society, and defendant's father was insured in that society. On the 23rd December the complainant called at the defendant's house in the course of his business, whereupon the defendant called him bad names and charged him with having lobbed persons of money. She also accused him of having forged a poet office order. To each of these accusations the complainant gave an emphatic denial. The defendant was bound over, herself in £l.O, and two sureties of £5 each, to keep the peace for three months.

BOARD OF GDARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting of this board was held on Thursday, Mr. Hall presiding. The Workhouse Master reported that there were last week 450 inmates of the house, the week previous exactly the same number, and in the corresponding month last year 479. A letter was read from the Supetioress of the Pantasaph Or- phanage stating that some very satisfactory letters had been received from the girls who had emigrated to Canada. The Clerk reported that since the last meeting he had seen Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, who wished to know whether persons who chanced to be taken suddenly ill were required in the first instance to get an order from the relieving officer before they could obtain the attendance of the medical officer. He (the clerk) assured Mr. Brighouse that in the Pres- cot union the medical officers were only too pleased to at- tend urgent cases without the official order. (Hear, hear.) On the suggestion of the clerk it was decided to paint the names and addresses of the medical officers on the windows of the relieving•officers for the guidance of persons when the offices were closed, and it was also resolved that a printed list of the names and addresses of the medical officers, to- gether with the names of their substitutes, he forwarded to each overseer and guardian of the union.

The INlaiquis of Salibury bas returned his tenants 15 per cent of their rents. . The constituents of Mr. Healy, M.P., on Tuesday pre- sented him with a cheque for £l,OOO. At the Cabinet Council, which eat for nearly three hours, the only Ministers absent were Mr. Gladstone and Earl Spencer. Poecnrien ATFRAT.—A desperate poaching affray took place near Broabourne early on Tuesday morning between three poachers and several gamekeepers. Two keepers and One porcher were seriously injured. Two poachers were arrested.

Sir,—Your correspondent; •• Clifford. Dix„" whoever he rase be, really is entitled to a premium for the manner in which he keeps your readers supplied with ideas If, how- ever, he would adhere to his own ideas and always write consistently with his previously expressed (minions, we could better understand the object he shIS at, which at present is not very clear. Does he wish all men ta be equal in possessions ? Because if he entertains such a desire it will never be gratified. There never was equality of posi- tion, and there never will be, either in this or in any other country. If your correspondent is posseseed of an cbserv- ing nature he will have seen ample reason for this during the past fortnight, even if there did not exist any further reason. Suppose every man in Warriorton had Zrf), given to him by the Government (a very unlikely circumstance) this January, what ace would the majority make of it? Would it be increased, or would it have altogether dis- appeared by next January ? Your correspondent refers to the wealth of the Crawshays ; he referred to the position of the Rylanc:s family in a previous letter, but the Rylands family had as small a begin- ning as the modest sum I have named. Why, then envy them of the fruit of their energy ? They have lived in prosperous times when the introduction of steam power to machinery has made more fortunes than ever were m 'de in the same time b:fore. But your correspon- dent told us in a previous letter that manufacturers were now barely getting change for a shilling, and I dare say Rylands Brothers would confirm this statement respecting • the present profits upon trade. ledeed, Mr. Peter Rylands had the courage to tell Mr. Gladstone as much in the House of Commons only a few weeks ago. But persona who have made money in the past, when England was the workshop of the world, have invested much of their earnings in foreign securities as they saw the possible decline of British indus- • tries, and so placed their eggs in different baskets, making I themselves independent of circumstances. Your correspondent writes foolishly when he deprecates the extension of industrial occupations, for where would the ' ever-increasing population find employment if it was not for ' the extension of old works, or the starting of new ones? Indeed} the possibility of curtailment constitutes the prin- cipal danger to our working population in the future, The most sensible sentence written by your correspon• dent is where he remarks "I am sadly afraid that, whilst we are spending blood and treasure in putting other lands

to right, we are'neglecting our own;" but tbi3 is not a very I complimentary, opinion to express respecting the present I Government , The year 1884 is now numbered with the past The year will be remembered by many throughout England; wages have been reduced without any corresponding gain, and there does net appear much hope of recovering what has been lost. Indeed the probability Is that further concessions will have to be made to meet the increaeing foreign compe- tition, for we may be sure that inanufac'nrers will not run their mills simply to find employment for tins working pepulation. Free Trade or Fait Trade manufecturers are , fairly entitled to a profit upon their invested capital, and management in the collection and working of a business. During the past year, England has had corn at a lower price than ever it was known before, but it has made little little difference in the price of bread, say one h dfpenny per loaf, amid if all the land in England was almlutely rent free this year, it would not make more than another half-penny par loaf difference, because corn being so low in value British farmers cool .1 fi,.d batter markets abroad, and they would naturally sell in the best market. Besides who is to say, under such revolutionary doctrines as those put forward by Mr. Henry George, which particular man has a right to cer- -1 tain land? The owner certainly has the best right; after I this it might be a fight eternally for possession. But land cannot be free either in tbie or any other country ; it be- ca o mr reasonable ov na al valuable ed ea 0niZ2..i.7,r otme c al m prosperousu s tart Ce, and mim lenduf withc tur niga , locality is most valuable. Land has its value quite an much as houses or other possessions, and the law which disturbs one will, in time, unsettle the other.

We have now cheap corn and the farmer injured; sugar cheap and the industry ruined; wire cheap and wages re- duced 25 per cent, and so on, all through the whole produc- ing and industrial population. The reduction of .1-d per loaf is a miserable set off against a redaction of five shil- lings per week in the rate of wages, and another five shil- lings lost through short time occasioned by the foreigner having got the orders which British worl3men ought to have been employed with. And who does all this benefit the most? Simply mere theorists, newspaper men, mer- chants, lawyers, and independent gentlemen living upon incomes derived from foreign investments in Egyptian bonds, Mexican railways, American companies, ate. Lin fortunately these men predominate in the British House of Commons at the present time. Look at its composition, and you find 7 iron masters and 33 m mufacturers ; "but what are they amongst so many ? " Where es you find 51 mer- chants and 113 railway ram. How on earth do the manu- facturers and workmen of England hope to ever get the railway rates reduced if they send these men to Parliament? If we adopt a policy which encourages foreign competition, we most take all the consequences of that carepstition—loss of orders, want of employment, reduction of wages, &c, and so help to increase the boundary of that miserable picture to which your correspondent now 'alludes, but to which Fair Traders have long ago drawn at- tention, when he states—"ln a sketch of travels recently issued, the writer asserts that in none of the countries to which we send missionaries are the poor in such an abject Condition as we see them in the back slums of our own large towns." It may truly be said of Free Traders, "Out of their own mouth will I condemn them." Give these miserable unemployed people in our back streets work and wages; then teach them self-respect, and you will remove the sight of each a picture as the one alluded to. But you must first modify a policy which takes the work and wages away from our workmen and ainks them in obscurity; but which gives orders, employment, and wages to the workmen of foreign lands.—Yours truly. FAIR PROFIT. Warrington, 6th January, 1885.

REDISTRIBUTION AND THE WORKING CLASSES. Sir,—Shakespeare says, "There is a tide in the affairs of men, which taken at the flood leads on to fortune." The extension of the suffrage to the householdets in the coun- ties and the imminent redistribution of seats may be looked upon as the flowing of that tide in the political affairs of EnglisOmen, which, if taken advantage of, may lead on to the deliverance of the hitherto umepreeented, if not mis- represented, working classes from a thraldotn almost too bitter to be borne. Up to the present, the electors among , , the working classes in large towns have been completely I absorbed In one or other of the great political parties. It is surprising that since their enfranchisement in 1367 the working classes have not done anything in the interest of their order commensurate with the political power which was then placed in their hands. The reason of this may be that the skilful working of the Caucus by both Liberals and Conservatives has reduced that power to a minimum, and, lacking leaders in whom they could place confidence, the voters among the working classes have been absorbed in the rank and file of the two parties, with the exception of the disciples of dynamite who are too outrageous for either ' party to deal with. The working clasees preponderate in all boroughs; it is , therefore not too much to say that they were the means of 'returning the Parliaments of 1863.1874, and 1330, com- posed, with the exception of Messrs Macdonald, Burt, and Broadhurst, of men out of sympathy with, if not entirely Opposed to their own order, viz., those who live by manual labour. Is it anything to wonder at that their interests are continually sacrificed when, in their folly they have sent to Parliament hundreds of lawyers and landlords, military officers, and millowners, railway director, and stockholders It is only natural that these monied and professional classes should legislate in the interests of the upper and middle classes, while the working classes, the backbone of the country, are elbowed out of every good thing, and have to take what they can get, in the same spirit as a dog who has a bone thrown to him. Look at the way taxation is shifted from the shoulders of the ruling classes and placed on the poorer classes. Tea is the poor man's beverage, while champagne is the popular drink of the rich. One would think that a rich man could better afford to pay an extra tax on his beverage than the poor man on his homely tea, but the reverse is the case. The taxation on a shillingsworth of tea is eightpence, that on a shillingsworth of champagne is one halfpenny ! Poor people have to rent houses. Rich landlords receive ground rents. In our innocence we would have thought that the rich man would be called upon to pay more as the owner of land than the owner of the house property who has to rely on his poor tenants for his income. Once more the reverse is the case. The taxation on £lOO worth of house property is forty shillings per annum ; that on £l.OO worth of ground rents is one shilling and threepence per annum! A large proportion of the two millions, to be enfranchised on the let of January 1836 are working men, and my object in writing is to endeavour to pursued° my fellow working- men to look after their own interests in political matters. This can only be done by holding aloof from the caucus; more especially the Tory caucus, whose most active agents are the soup and blanket clergymen of the so-called " Church of England," and those " artists in human slaughter"—the grog-sellers. The working men have been bamboozled by both parties too long for them to have any faith in either, and I have studied them to a little purpose if I have not found out that they are not likely again to sell their votes for a beggarly bowl of soup or a Dot of beer. Besides turning a deaf ear to the hypocritical blandish- ments of the place-hunting parties, the working classes should bring out candidates of their own—either members of their own order, or men in sympathy with their views and aims In this way alone can their claims be en- forced. The loudest politician has the best chance of being heard. This has been clearly proved by the dynamite party of late and with a roach better cause than the Nationalist noodles, there is the greater probability of their influence being felt for good. How will the coming alteration in the distribution of political power affect us—the working-men of the Runcorn district ? Are we, as working-men, to be handed over in a body to what is called the Liberal party, to be represented by some successful manufacturer or needy politician from one of the London clubs, either of whom would tread wit' the lesiat compunction on the aspirations and interests of the working classes, without whose votes they would not have the ghost of a chance of being returned ? Or are we, to form ourselves into an independent party and bring out an Industrial candidate? To the first question I should return an emphatic" no." There is some difficulty in an-

RUNCORN AND WIDNES. RUb CORN SCHOOL BOARD: The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednes- day, at the office,Bridgewater-street. Mr. J. Prichard occu- pied /lac chair, and there were also present Messrs. Lea, Briscoe, Norman, and F. Rigby (clerk), and F. Holme (architect). Tun PROPOSED New Sowoom—Contracts for the pro- posed new school in Orreenway-road bad been received from the following :—Morrison and Son, Wavertree ; John Acton and, Son, Knutsford ; Thomas Roberts, St. Helens; Thomas Damson, Liverpool; Wm. Brown, &Ilford ; Thos. Tyson, Liverpool; WM. Farrell, Runcorn; Wm. Pcrter, Warring- ton ; and Wm. Winnard, Wigan. After considerable die- cuseion consideration of the tenders was deferred. EXTRAORDINARY ACTION OE/ TUB SCHOOLSIASTERS.—The 'Clerk made a statement with regard to the admission of children into school. There was the case of a boy named Wright. At the School Attendance Committee meeting, on the 3rd December, his parent stated that he had been re- I fused admimion at the various boys' schools. Bowyer had made inquiries, and Le had reported that he found the state- ment made by the mother to be true, and the boy could not get into a school anywhere in Runcorn. The head masters of the National and the Weeleyan schools said they had re- fused to admit the boy during the week ending the sth December bereuee he had left Trinity boys' school during the same week. The mother then made application to the head master of Trinity boys' school for re-admission, and he refused because the boy had left his school the previous week:, and hed been seeking admission in another school. The consequence was that the boy could rot get into ene of. the three schools in Runcora which were available. He Ness eight years of age, and was still absent. Bowyer was simply pone-flees. Na pressure could be put upon the paronte. It would be obviously the duty of the magistrates to irquire whether admission had been refused, and if the boy was not admitted the Bench would not punish him. What WAS the Board to do ? The clerk read extracts from the Act bearing upon the subject, and asked—lf you sam- men a child for not going to schoel regularly, and the parent says the child is refused admission, what are you to do ?—Mr. Norman: I cannot say what you can do in the case. You should deal with the echoolmasters.—The Clerk : That is the only way we can do, but we have no power over the schoolmasters, as they told us on one occa- sion me could report to the Education department that the masters of three schools ref used admission to this child. —Mr. Norman : If you write to the Department they will communicate at once with the school-masters, won't they? —The Clerk : Oh, certainly.—Mr. Norman : Get them into trouble, that's it —The Cerk: If the Board autho- rises me I will lay the case before the Department.—Mr. Norman : That is the only step we can take.—The Clerk: I think so.—The Chairman asked whether it would not be best to first represent the c ase to the masters.—The Clerk: It has been represented to them, I thiuk. They had been seen on several occaeions by Bowyer.—Mr. Norman thought it was very wrong of Mr. Annett not to take the lad back.— Mr. Lea : He left of his own accord. Why should not the other masters take him as soon as Mr. Annett.—Mr. Nor- man Because be was a regular scholar of Mr. Annett's.—Mr. Lea They have more room at the Wesleyan School than we have at Trinity.—Mr. Norman: I thought there was another case, Mr. Clerk 7—The Clerk replied that that was sub-judice.—Mr. Norman, referring to the Chairman's sug- gestion, said they might send Bowyer to tell the masters that if they did not admit the boy they would write to the Education Department.—Mr. B ovver : A letter from the Board would be much better than me going—Tire Clerk : It will only involve as in a long correspondence with the teachers, and we should probably have a deputation from them and be told as we were on a previous occasion that they had nothing to do with the Education Department.—' The Chairman said at the laet committee meeting several boat people attended and stated that they and their families Went periodic ally away from home. They shut up their houses, and had no means of leaving their children in the town. On their return some of the children who had been in the habit of attending Trinity School were sent there, and they were told that they would have to be subjected to double flee. The children were also sect to other scheels as well and they were refused admittance though there was room for them. They then went to Bowyer and asked what they could do. Of course the Board was put in a very peculiar position and was unable to help the parents out of the difficulty. This double fee of course was a bar to the admission of the children, and as the parents stated, they could not eff ed to pay it, and they looked upon it as a hardship that the chil- dren were not admitted to any school. Such action as this really frustrated the work of the Board in getting the chil- dren of the town educated. The matter had really become a serious one. If it was decided to write to the education department the whole facts ought to be described. It was not one case alone but many.—Mr. Norman : Are we to understand that these teachers have said distinctly that they have nothing to do with the education department? —The Clerk : One said so in this room. Didn't you bear it Mr. Lea ?—Mr. Lea : Yee.—Mr. Norman: Best plan will be to write then.—Mr. Briscoe concurred.—Mr. Lea was also in favour of this course to get the thing settled. It Was no use beating about the bush.—lt was then decided that the Clerk should forward a ceminunicedon to the Education Department on the subject. There WAS no other business of public importance. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday. Present —the Rev. John Lockwood, Messrs John Ashton (chair. man), Aaron, Stokes, Hall, P. Speakman, W. Handley, W. Whittaker, C. Rigby, Weir, Lewis, Pickering, Mclntyre, Whitlow, H. Linker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy *clerk). FINANCE.—The Rev. J. Lockwood presented the report of the Finance Committee who recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £314 15s 7d.—Carried. THE FREEING OE DBE BELIDGIC, Mr. Aaron inquired whether any reply had been received from the Mayor of Chester with regard to this subject. In addition to taking that £l,OOO how much had the corporation of Chester taken from the ratepayers in getting the Act. Where did the money come from.—The Clerk : The Chester people bear the expense of the Act.—Mr. Annan : Are you certain of that. —The Clerk: Oh yes.—Mr. Aaron : That's right. I beg to move that we write to the Local Uoverument Board and see whether we cannot get an answer from them as to 1 what Denbigh and Flint pay. What is the Duke I of Westminster or the Towle Clerk that we should be insul- ted 7—Mr. C. Rigby (impressively) : He's a rich man.— The Chalrnan rernarkAl that the matter had nothing to do • -with the Local Government Board.—Mr. Aaron : The poor farmers have great difficulty in scratching their rates and tithes together without paying a thousand pounds—Mr. C. Rigby : That's true, Aaron! There's no doubt about that. —Mr. Aaron again moved that the Local Government Board be addressed on the subject, but there were many expres- sions of dissent. —The Rev. J. Lockwood observed that a reply would probably be received by the next meeting, and Mr. Aaron resumed his seat. Tan Paoriecriort OF ens bloom—Mr. Handley slid the Visiting Committee bad considered the scheme of Messrs ,C. Linaker and Davies for protecting the House in case of fire. They thonght the scheme a very good one and that the parts of the house would be protected with a little additional hose to cover the vagrants and receiving wards. -This alteration would perhaps increase the cost irom £325 to £350. The committee therefore recommended that the fire appliances as proposed in the report referred to be pro- vided with sufficient additional hose to protect the vagrant -and receiving wards, and that the cost be spread over a period of ten years by borrowing the money, to be repaid by half-yearly instalments of principal and interest —Mr. Aaron emended the proposition, and spoke of the necessity of the appliances.—Mr. Handley said it was proposed to 'piece 10 hydrants in different parts of the premises, so that there wouldbe no carriage of water required if a fire should un- fortunately break out-Mr. Whitlow proposed an amendment that the subject should be postponed indefinitely. If a fire should unfortunately arise there were not half a dozen people in the house who would not run away as scones they Meld, and a great many of the inmates were incapable of wr eking the hydrants if they were Inclined to do so. Be- sides he thought that this was a very bad time to bring for- I Ward such a scheme, because money was very difficult to get, and he pointed out that there was a very efficient fire I engine and brigade at Preston Brook ready for operations whenever called upon.—Mr. Aaron said anyone who could use one hand could put out a fire by the scheme proposed. He did not know what the Preston Brook engine was like now, but some years ago he had a fire, and the Preston Brook engine was not worth anything.—Mr. C. Rigby seconded the amendment.—Mr. 'Mclntyre inquired whether other workhouses had similar appliances for ,putting out fire.—The Clerk could give no information on the subject. —Mr. Aaron said at Prescot they had spent several thousand pounds on a scheme.—lt was eventually unani- mously decided to postpone consideration of the scheme, the clerk in the meantime to communicate with the Locel Government Board and iaquire whether they would sanction money to carry it out. THE VAGRANCY Noteemcg.—Mr. P. Speakman Introduced thr subject of vagrancy. He said under a general of the Local Government Board, vagrants who entered the house hap their supper, went to bed and next morning they were given 411 as. of rope to make into oakum. Mr. Jones infor- med him that some of the vagrants were three days in com- pleting their task. Now, at Chester the proceris of breaking stones were carried out. The vagrants had a certain quantity to break before they were permitted to go out ;1 and this was very much harder work than picking oakum. Consequently there were less applicants to Chester ward than there were to those where they had to be kept so long a time. He therefore proposed that the subject should be re- ferred to the House Committee for their consideration.—Mr Wair descrioed the arrangements for vagrants at Preston, of which he spoke in commendatory terms, and Mr. Intyre said tbe laturee in which stme breaking had to be performed were always given a wide berth by the tramping fraternity —The motion was carried.
APPOINTMENT.—Mr. Percy Rindall, Legh-street, has been appointed organist and choirmaster of St. Annes' Church.
SUDDEN DEVTII —The infant daughter of a man named Coles, living in Dallam-lane, died on Thursday in con- vulsions.

BEATA FROM 13ZRNS.—A boy named Michael Kelly, son of Michael and Ann Kelly, of Phillip-street, off Charles street, died OR Thursday from injuries received the previous day, when he was severely burned. He was left in the house with two sisters on Wednesday by the mother, who west to the market, and as he was playing with a piece of lighted paper his pinafore caught fire and he was enveloped in flames. The poor little fellow ran out of the house and a neighbour threw something over hire, which stifled the dunes. Dr. Adams subsequently saw the deceased, who was shockingly burned, and held out uo hopes of his re- covery. The father is a forgeman at DaDam. BraTONWOOD.—Parish Church: On New Year's Eve a tea party and ball were held in the c'eurch schoolroom, Burtonwood. About 400 sat down to tea. The schoolroom was appropriately decorated for the occasion. Dancing was kept up to the strains of Mr. Appleton's band, comprising cornopeii, harp, and violin. The proceeds were to defray the expenses incurred in repairing the church.— Wesleyan Sunday School: The scholars' annual tea party was held in the chapel on New Year's Day. After tea Mr. Jas. Wright presided. The report read by the secretary, Mr. R. Sims, showed that the echolars on the books were—boys 39, girls 40; and the finances revealed wa balance in the treasurer's hands of £2 18s 9d. A brief address was delivered by the chairman, after whichneveral dialogues were given, in which the following took part: Messrs T Travis, E Broster, H Jones, B Sims, J Ashton, W Jones, Mrs A Sims. Mrs M Sims, Mies H Fester, Miss E Foster, Miss K Foster, Miss M Sims, Miss A Travis, and Miss 8 Ratcliffe. Recitations were given by Miss B Travis, John Travis, Katie Foster, Walter Hewitt, Alfred Honghton, William 110thwell, Thos. Hewitt, Sarah Hewitt. Songs by Miss M elms, Miss E Foster, and Mr R Sims. Several selections were also rendered be the choir. Prizes, consisting of hooks, were pr,sented for good attendance to 57 scholars. The catering , and cutting up for the tea was done by Mrs Sims, Mrs Houghton, and Mrs Makin. The singing of the Doxology concluded the meeting'

ARBITRATION BETTER THAN WAR. LIBERAL LECITAR AT RUNCORN. Under the auspices of the Runcorn Liberal AsFociation, the Rev. Joseph Freeston, of the Lancashire and Yorkshire International Arbitration Association, delivered a lecture in B3thesda School-room, Runcorn, on Thursday evening, On the subject of "Arbitration Better than War." Mr. B Xiiveton, who etas accompanied by Mr. 0. Leak, occupied the chair. The attendance was not so large as might have been expected from the reputation of the lecturer, but the lecture was listened to with intelligent attmtion from the conar.lencement to the finish.—The Chairman in- trnduc, d the lectmer in a brief but appropriate speech. scrmence of the newly-acquired power of the working man WIDNES LOCAL BOARD AND THE through the passing of the Franchise Bill, and asserted that MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. under a democracy there ought to be fewer wars than we bad hitherto engaged in. FRODSFIIII- - DittliEni.—We understand that the Rev. Canon Barclay hes found it necessary to resign the office of Rural Dun of Frodshain, and the Rev. Canon Greenelt. SALE OF WORK.—A Christmas tree and silo of work has i been held in the schoolroom adjoining the Primitive Metho- dist Chapel at Prodsham Bridge, the opening ceremony b&n.; gracefully performed by Mit. White. of RunCern, who made a few appropriate remarks, and contributed £5 towards the funds, which, it was announced, are for the purpose of ; paying the expenses incurred in repairing the roof of the I chapel, and reducing the debt. PAROCHIAL TEA AND CONCEILT.—The annual parochial tea party and concert in connection with the Froistiam Parish Church took place in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday. About 280 persons sat down to tea, and the fol- lowing ladies presided at the tables :—Mesdames H. Li aaker, Reynolds, C. Linaker, Ashton, Sutton, Tomlinson, Thomas, , Hutchings, Bate, Dunsford, and Hitchen ; and Misses Cress- field, Ashley, Davies, Clarke, and Hitchen. At the concert in tbe evening there was a good attendance, and those who took pert in the programme were, with one or two excep. tions, members of the Parish Church choir. Mr. Thomas Riley was the conductor, and Mr. Charles Riley presided at the piano. LIAVINGS' Besit.—The sixty-third annual general meeting of the trustees and managers of the above institution was held in the Town Hall, Frodsharn, on Tuesday, when Mr. Charles Reynolds presided. Mr. John Pollard, secretary, submitted the accounts for the past v.ar, which had been audited and certified as correct by Mr. James Rigby, from which we extract the following, viz :—Receipts : Balance at commencement of the year, £21,565 18e lid ; received from depositors, £3,245 334 d ; interest, £638 175—£25,449 19e 34. Payments : To depositors, £4,159 63 id; manage- ment expenses, £73 3s 7d; balance at end of the year, £21.217 4s 7d, The report was adopted, and managers were appointed for the ensuing year. TREAT TO OLD PEOFLE.—A pleasant time was spent by some of the old people of Frodeham on Thursday week, when, by the kind invitation of Mr. and Ma. Charlee E. Linaker, a tea was provided in the Town Hall, Frodshaie, for all the old men and women residing in Frodsham and Frothleam Lordship in receipt of parish relief. A number of ladies and gentlemen were most assiduOus ire their atten- tion to the guests. After tea a programme of music and reading was successfully gone through by Miss K. S. Rigby, Mr. John Rigby, Mr. B. Rigby, Master Harry Linaker, and Mr. W. Cameron; Lancashire readings by Mr. H. Linaker, and pianoforte solos by the Misses Rigby and Master Albert Walker. Oranges, apples, and cokes were afterwards distri- buted, and Mrs. H. Linaker gave each person a packet of tea and a mince pie. PRODSHAN PAROCHIAL COMHITTEE.—A spectal meeting of the above committee was held in the Town Hall, Fred- sham, on Monday evening, when Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., pee- sided.—The Clerk read a report from Mr. Henry Boma t, engineer, of Manchester, in reference to the test pumping at trial wells at Newton, in which he stated—" I regret to ' report that the ganaings during the pest week of the water yielded by the two wells are very considerably below that of September and October last. Well No. I was 3,614 gal- lons in 24 hours, and well No. 2 2,948. These gave a reduc- tion of 72 per cent. in well 1, and 46 per cent, in well No. 2. This diminution is undoubtedly caused by the last two excessive dry season% we have had, and to some extent it will have been influenced by the frost. The rainfall during the past two months does not appear to hove penetrated the ground more than two or three feet. I have during the past week also gauged the springs on Mr. Wright's land, from which you originally intended tailing the water, and find a !similar reduction there ; the yield now Is only 8,754 gallons in 24 hours. These springs were ganged from March, 1879, to March, 1884, and the minimum yield recorded during that period was 14,975 gallons in 24 hours, while the maximum was 98,051 gallons in the same time, being a reduction of 41.5 per cent, on the minimum, and 63 per cent, on the maximum yield. The disproportions between the canines of the water in the two wells is caused to a great extent by the loss of water down the borehole in well No. 1. This was proved by the water in the borehole standing all the week at one foot below the bottom of the well, and on Saturday when the well and pumps were lowered 10. inches. The water in the borehole whilst the pumping was going on was lowered in the same proportion, whilst the well yielded the same quantity of water. lam of opinion that with an average rainfall sufficient water can be met with on the late Major Ilitchen'e land, but it is evident that further provision than was intended will have to be made for storing water to pro- vide for a supply during such a drought as we have had for the last two seasons." Mr. Bancroft suggested in his report that the borehole should be hermetically sealed and the bottom of No. I well paved, and a wall built to level of heading, also to make open cuttings from the same well, 15 feet deep in a westerly and southerly direction.—The re- port of Mr. Bencroft was accepted, hut previous to carry- ing out his suggestions, it was decided to test the yield of water from boring in No. 1 well, by continuous pumping for 48 hours, and to pave the bottom of the well.—The meet- ing was ad.'. nirned for this work to be done.

DISORDERLY ON LICENSED PREMISES.—At Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a young man named Patrick Donough was fined 5s and cuss for refusing to quit ' the Wellington Hotel, Earlestown, in November last. It appeared that he was very quarrelsome, and a constable had to be sent for. He failed to answer the summons, and a warrant was issued in consequence. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT CROFT.—On Thursday evening week, soon after seven o'clock, a blacksmith named Corne- lius Unsworth, residing near the Smithy-brow, Croft, at- tempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat with a razor. It appeared that Dr. Sephton saw him on Thursday morning, and said he must be carefully watched. About seven o'clock in tbe evening, as he was seated by the fire- side, he commenced talking in a strange manner, threaten- ing to kill his wife and children. They ran for assistance, and while they were away Unsworth cut his throat from left to right, inflicting a wound about four inches long. He threw a lighted paraffin lamp, which was burning on the table, into the pool of blood which had flowed from the wound. The cut is a deep one, and has been stitched up by Dr. Sephton, who is still in attendance. Unsworth has been cvefully wa,ched since the occurrenc,, as he seems determined to destroy himself, and is obviously suffering from temporary insanity. TEL PARTY AT Srocrc-rosz UV:Tn.—The annual tea party in connection with the IRdependent Methodist Chapel, Stockton Heath, was held on Monday, when over 200 sat down to tea. Afterwards a very profitable and interesting miscellaneous entertainment was given, and was more numerously attended than on previous similar occasions. The meeting was presided over by Mr. Joseph Mounfield, of Warringtcn. The programme consisted of songs and solos, which were rendered in excellent style by the Misses Critch- ley and Whitley, and also by Mrs. Isherwood, and the Messrs. Worsleys, Shaw, and Goodier. The recitations, which were given by. Mr Josiah Furness, of Warrington, followed by scholars of the Sabbath school, were given in a very creditable manner. The choir sang with sweet- ness and precision, showing careful training on the part of Mr. Peter Harrison, who also presided at the harmonium, in.l showed marked efficiency. After a vote of thanks had deen given to the chairman and others, the meeting was tyought 0 3 close by singing the doxology.

ton went to church a alection was made in support of i. ([leer, hear.), He did not know that the Church ever did a better work than when it lent its aid and its

power in support of the orphan and of the fatheriess. (Ap- plause.) The Custnadalt in responding, said he did not pretend to enter into any argument whether the school was doing sufficient work or not, hut the trustees were certainly doing I their best to make the school a useful one to the town.

There was one point which he had noticed. and which pro- I bably Mr. Mbnks had not considered when making his speech, and that was that they must not forget that the trustees could not go beyond the powers granted to them without first °Staining an act of Porliament.. Of course, if, . . .

as Mr. Monks suggested, the school were assisted by volun- tary contributions, the trustees would have more money to spend, and more scholars and orphans would 139 educ del He believed the trustees did all they could with the funds at
their disposal, to promote the interests of the children, who were propenry looked after. (Hear, hear.), If the trustees could obtain money. to enlarge the school, and do some _ . .

good, he, ea one of the trustees, wonld be thankful; at the same time-they must give the children a. religious and moral education. That, he was fatly convinced,, was the duty of the trustees of the foundation, and he believed they had never swerved from it. (Applause.) Alderman Davres, in also reeponding, said that for many years the objects of this charity weranot devoted exactly as they were required under the Acts of Parliament or what they Galled the schemes of the charity. For many years in connection with that school there were what they called dr-y boys, of which he was one himeat. He had no doubt Ma. Thbert Davies would recollect the time when that school was doing a greater work than what it was te.day. Ilear, hear.) At that time it edecated 120 day boys in addition to the other boys in the school. A challenge wae made as to whether they were not exceeding the power of the trust and an inquiry was made, the result of which was that the 120 boys wore swept away from being educated under the objects of that charity. They were then confined simply to the boys immediately under the foundation. That was a great misfortune. (Hear, hear.) At that time—and it was no reflection upon the young men who went to the Boteler Grammar School—the Blue Coat Scheel was as I much regarded as the Grammar School, but the result oi the inquiry was that they were not allowed to have any more day boys. He believed those who caused the inquiry to be instituted were very sorry that it put an end to that education, but it was well to remember that in foundation schcola they were obliged to give an education which came within the four corners of ehe soheme. He„ however, should be pleased if an attempt was made to make the school one to give educa- tion to day boys in addition to those immediately under the foundation. (Applause) Dr. WHITE proposed the toast of "The Mayor and Cor- poration of Warrington." In referring to the work of the Corporation he said that in representative bodies, as in pri- vate families, there was often a black sheep, a spendthrift, and if he spoke of one committee as the prodigal, they would all know thtt he was referring to the Sanitary Com- mittee. As a humble follower of science, he was always glad to read of the costly experiments that were being made as to the best mode of the disposal of sewage, but as a rate- payer, and especially at the times when those little slips of blue paper called demand notes were handed round, he could have wished that the Sanitary Committee of War- rington had left such pursuits to better end swel communi- ties. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR, in responding, said he should think that from a sanitary point of view Warrington stood almost pre- eminent among the different towns—at the head of the list ; and notwithstanding they were somewhat hard upon thee Sanitary Committee sometimes, and still more so v.tieh refer- ence to that salubrious spot at Longford--.(iebghter)—yet he believed the Sani;a7; Committee were al)out to carry eut a great achievement.--a great success, and a plan that Iwould be followed by most corporate bodies in England. IThey knew perfectly well that the Corporation of Warring.; ten had been nuking efforts for a considerable time past for the purpose of making Warrington a model town, both with respect to sanitation and education. 'They had now the centre' of the educetioq department 90 far as regarded what were called the wits and strap, and he was afraid ' they would shortly have a School Board established in War- rington. ("No' no.") He had been told that the accom- modation tgr school purposes was now such as to absolve them from the immunity they had enjoyed from the expense of a School Board. He should be sorry to see a Schoal Board—(hear, hear)—and he hoped they would all support those educational institutions existing in the town in such a way as to render a School Board unnecessary. (Ap- plause.) However, this was a matter open for discussion. (Applause) A euphonium solo was then given in so excellent a Way by Mr. R. Anderton as to win an encore. The subs-qaent toasts were "The NVarrineton Blue Coat Brotherly Society," proposed by Mr. T. Morris, and responded to by Mr. Forshavr and Mr. Percival; "The Press," proposed by the Chairman, and duly responded to ; and "The Chairman," proposed by Mr. Percival, and responded to by the Cbairman.—The p-oceedings then ter- minated.

On Tuesday night the annual tea meeting was held in the school, when there were about 200 old Blues and friends present. The tea was under the superintendence of Mr. E. Rose and Mrs. Rose. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs. Fairclough, Mrs. Rose, Mts. Shaw, Mrs. Smith, Mrs. Forshaw, Mrs. Rigby, and Miss Craik. The majority of the members of the School Committee were in attendance. After tea the younger children amused them- selves by indulging in various games, whilst the elder ones engaged in dancing, Mr. Whittaker playing the concertina. During the evening the children were regaled with cake and nuts kindly given by Mr. Percival, chairman of the School Committee.
